Ka_C01_S01_INTRO1::block-0: Om. Salutations to the Lord Vaivasvata, who is Death, the teacher of the knowledge of Brahman, and to Naciketas.
Ka_C01_S01_INTRO1::block-1: Now, in order to easily expound the meaning of the vallīs of the Kāṭhakopaniṣad, a brief commentary is begun. The word 'upaniṣad' is derived from the root 'sad', which means 'to loosen', 'to attain' and 'to weaken', preceded by the prefixes 'upa' and 'ni' and ending with the suffix 'kvip'. By the word 'upaniṣad' is meant the knowledge that has for its object the Reality to be known, which is sought to be expounded by the text. By what etymological connection, then, is knowledge denoted by the word 'upaniṣad'? It is being explained: those seekers of liberation who, becoming free from craving for the objects seen here and heard of in the scriptures, having approached and resorted to the knowledge designated by the word 'upaniṣad' (whose characteristics will be stated), cultivate it with steady conviction — for them, knowledge is called upaniṣad because, by this etymological connection, it loosens, destroys and annihilates avidyā and the rest, the seed of saṃsāra. Thus too will it be said: 'Knowing him, one is freed from the jaws of death' (Ka. U. 1.3.15). Or else, since it leads the seekers possessed of the aforesaid qualities to the supreme Brahman, knowledge of Brahman is upaniṣad by virtue of its connection with leading-to-Brahman. Thus too will it be said: 'Having attained Brahman he became free from passion and free from death' (Ka. U. 2.3.18). Or, the knowledge concerning Agni, the first-born of Brahman who is the source of the worlds — sought through the second boon, conducing to the attainment of the heavenly world as its fruit — by virtue of its weakening (avasādayitṛtva) the host of afflictions of dwelling in the womb, birth, old age and the like that recur again and again in other worlds, is also called upaniṣad on account of its connection with the meaning of the root. Thus too will it be said: 'The dwellers in heaven attain immortality' (Ka. U. 1.1.13) and so on. But, it may be objected, students also speak of the text by the word 'upaniṣad' — saying 'we study the upaniṣad' and 'we teach the upaniṣad'. There is no fault here; for since the meanings of the root 'sad'—loosening of the causes of saṃsāra such as avidyā—are not possible in the mere text, but are possible in knowledge, the text too can be designated by that word as a means thereto, just as in 'Ghee verily is life' (Tai. Saṃ. 2.3.11) and the like. Therefore, the word 'upaniṣad' applies primarily to knowledge, and only secondarily to the text. Thus, by the very explanation of the word upaniṣad, the qualified aspirant for knowledge has been indicated. The subject too has been stated as the supreme Brahman that is the inmost Self. The purpose of this knowledge is the absolute cessation of saṃsāra, characterised by attainment of Brahman. The relation has been stated through this very purpose. Hence these vallīs, which manifest the knowledge endowed with the aforesaid qualified aspirant, subject, purpose and relation — as a fruit (āmalaka) placed on the palm — possess these same features. Therefore we explain them according to our understanding.
Ka_C01_S01_V01: Vājaśravas, desiring (the fruit of sacrifice), gave away all his wealth. He had a son, by name Naciketas. (1)
Ka_C01_S01_V01::block-0: Here a story is told for the purpose of extolling knowledge. 'Uśan' means 'desiring'. 'Ha' and 'vai' are particles indicating the recollection of a past event. 'Vāja' means food; he whose fame (śravas) arose because of the giving of food and the like is 'Vājaśravas'; or the name may be used conventionally. His son is 'Vājaśravasa'. That Vājaśravasa, it is said, performed the Viśvajit sacrifice in which all is offered, desiring its fruit. In that sacrifice he gave (dadau) all his wealth (sarvavedasam). Of that sacrificer there was a son named Naciketas — 'āsa' means 'there was'.
Ka_C01_S01_V02: When the gifts (cows) were being led away, faith entered him, who was still a boy. He thought: (2)
Ka_C01_S01_V02::block-0: Into him — Naciketas — though still a boy, of tender age, who had not yet attained the power of generation, faith (śraddhā), which is a sense of belief in the unseen, prompted by the desire for his father's welfare, entered. At what time? It is said: when the cows meant as gifts (dakṣiṇā) were being led away, being apportioned and brought severally to the ṛtviks and the assembly-members, then Naciketas, into whom faith had entered, reflected as follows.
Ka_C01_S01_V03: Their water drunk, their grass eaten, their milk milked dry, their senses gone — joyless indeed are those worlds to which he goes who gives such cows. (3)
Ka_C01_S01_V03::block-0: How? It is being said. The cows meant as dakṣiṇā are being qualified by the words beginning with 'pītodakāḥ'. Those by which water has been drunk are 'pītodakāḥ' — water-drunk. Those by which grass has been eaten are 'jagdhatṛṇāḥ' — grass-eaten. Those whose milking — namely, what is called 'milk' — has been done up are 'dugdhadohāḥ' — milked dry. 'Nirindriyāḥ' means incapable of generation, aged — useless cows is the meaning. Such cows being these, he, giving them to the ṛtviks with the thought that they are dakṣiṇā, goes to those worlds which are 'anandāḥ', that is, joyless, sorrowful — that sacrificer goes to those worlds.
Ka_C01_S01_V04: He said to his father: 'Father, to whom will you give me?' A second time and a third time he asked. To him his father said: 'To Death I give you.' (4)
Ka_C01_S01_V04::block-0: Thus thinking — 'the unwished-for fruit accruing to my father from the imperfection of the sacrifice should be averted by me, his son, even by the giving up of myself, having thereby completed the sacrifice perfectly' — he approached his father and said to him: 'O tāta (dear father), to which special ṛtvik will you give me as dakṣiṇā?' Though disregarded by his father when he had thus spoken, he asked a second time and a third time: 'To whom will you give me? To whom will you give me?' Angered, thinking 'this is not the nature of a boy', the father said to that son indeed: 'I give you to Death — to Vaivasvata.'
Ka_C01_S01_V05: Among many I go as the first; among many I go as middling. What duty of Yama is there, that he will accomplish through me today? (5)
Ka_C01_S01_V05::block-0: The son, thus addressed, lamented in solitude. How? It is said: 'Among many disciples or sons, I go as the first — that is, I conduct myself by the foremost manner of a disciple etc. And among the many middling ones, I go in middling fashion — by the middling conduct alone, never by the lower.' Yet the father said even of such a son endowed with distinguished qualities: 'I give you to Death.' What purpose of Yama will he indeed accomplish today through me, who have been given to him — what task is to be done? Surely the father has spoken thus through anger, without any regard for purpose. Even so, let not the father's word become false.
Ka_C01_S01_V06: Look back upon the ancestors, look forward upon those who came after. Like corn the mortal ripens; like corn he is born again. (6)
Ka_C01_S01_V06::block-0: Having so resolved, with grief he addressed his father, who was overcome with sorrow at what he himself had said: 'Look back (anupaśya), reflect, consider in due order how the ancients, your forefathers and grandfathers, conducted themselves; seeing them, you ought to follow their conduct. Look forward (pratipaśya) too at how the present-day saints behave. There has neither been nor is there in them any falsifying of word; the contrary is the conduct of the unrighteous — the falsifying of word. And no one, having spoken falsehood, becomes free from old age and death; for, like corn, the mortal — man — ripens, grows old and dies; and having died, like corn he is born again — comes forth once more. In such a transient world of living beings, what is gained by speaking falsely? Preserve your truthfulness. Send me to Yama' — this is the sense.
Ka_C01_S01_V07: Like Vaiśvānara (fire), the brāhmaṇa guest enters the house. For him men perform this propitiation. O Vaivasvata, fetch the water. (7)
Ka_C01_S01_V07::block-0: Thus addressed, the father sent him forth in order to keep his own truthfulness. He, having gone to Yama's abode and Yama being absent, dwelt there for three nights. When Yama returned from his absence, his ministers or his wife, addressing him by way of admonition, said: 'A brāhmaṇa, in the form of an atithi (guest), enters one's house as if it were Vaiśvānara — fire — itself, as though burning it. Quenching, as it were, the burning of that fire, good men perform for him this propitiation (śānti) characterised by the giving of water for the feet, a seat, and the rest, since he is a guest. Therefore, O Vaivasvata, fetch (hara) water, for the washing of Naciketas's feet.'
Ka_C01_S01_V08::block-0:
Since scripture declares that fault arises from failing to honour [a Brāhmaṇa guest], — āśā-pratīkṣe: 'āśā' is the longing for a desired object whose attainment is uncertain, and 'pratīkṣā' is the awaiting of an object whose attainment is certain; these two, hope and expectation; saṅgatam, the fruit born of association with the good; sūnṛtām ca, sweet and pleasant speech, and the fruit dependent thereon; iṣṭāpūrte, 'iṣṭa' meaning the fruit of sacrificial rites and 'pūrta' meaning the fruit of works such as making gardens, wells and the like; putra-paśūn ca, sons and cattle, all of these.

All this aforementioned, etat sarvaṁ vṛṅkte — he destroys, cuts off, brings to ruin. Of which person? Puruṣasya alpa-medhasaḥ, of the man of little intelligence, in whose house a Brāhmaṇa, anaśnan, going without food, dwells. The purport, therefore, is that under no circumstance whatsoever should a guest be slighted or neglected.
Ka_C01_S01_V09::block-0:
Thus addressed, Mṛtyu, approaching Naciketas with due reverence, said: — 'tisraḥ rātrīḥ yat avātsīḥ', because for three nights you have dwelt, gṛhe me, in my house, anaśnan, without taking food; he Brahman, O Brāhmaṇa, being a guest worthy of salutation, namasyaḥ, therefore namaḥ te astu, may obeisance be unto you. He Brahman, svasti me astu, may welfare be mine — that is, may there be release from the fault that arises from your having dwelt without food in my house.

Though by your grace alone, through the cessation of that lapse, all welfare would surely accrue to me, yet, in order to render you still more graciously disposed, vṛṇīṣva, choose, prati trīn varān, three boons, one for each of the three nights you have spent fasting — solicit from me objects of your wish.
Ka_C01_S01_V10::block-0:
Naciketas then says: — 'If you wish to grant boons, [grant me this:] śānta-saṅkalpaḥ, may my father be one whose anxious thoughts towards me are quieted — namely, the apprehension, ''Having gone to Yama, what now will my son do?'' — that anxious resolve having been pacified; sumanāḥ, of cheerful and serene mind; vīta-manyuḥ, with anger wholly gone; gautamaḥ, my father, may he be so disposed towards me, mā abhi, hē Mṛtyo.

Moreover, tvat-prasṛṣṭam, having been released and sent forth by you back to my home, mā abhivadet pratītaḥ — may he, his memory restored, address me, recognising me thus: ''This is indeed that very son of mine come back.'' This is the purport. Etat-prayojanam — for this end I crave, as the first of the three boons, the propitiation of my father.'
Ka_C01_S01_V11::block-0:
Mṛtyu replied: — 'yathā purastāt', as before — that is, the disposition that earlier subsisted in your father towards you, full of affection; bhavitā, will be — your father, full of love as before, will be pratītaḥ, recognising you. Auddālakiḥ — Uddālaka himself is Auddālaki; āruṇiḥ — son of Aruṇa; or alternatively a 'dvyāmuṣyāyaṇa' (one belonging by descent to two fathers).

Mat-prasṛṣṭaḥ, dismissed and sent forth by me, he will sleep through the remaining nights too, sukham, in tranquil and peaceful mind; vīta-manyuḥ, his anger gone; tvām dadṛśivān, beholding you his son, mṛtyu-mukhāt pramuktam, released from the very jaws of death.
Ka_C01_S01_V12::block-0:
Naciketas spoke: — 'svarge loke', in the heavenly world, na bhayaṁ kiñcana asti, there is no fear at all whatsoever, such as that arising from disease and the like. Nor, na tatra tvam, do you, O Death, hold sway there with sudden onslaught; therefore none in that world, beset with old age as in this world, fears you.

Moreover, ubhe — both — aśanāyā-pipāse, hunger and thirst, tīrtvā, having transcended, and going beyond grief — śokātigaḥ — devoid of mental anguish, modate, he rejoices and exults, svarga-loke, in the heavenly realm of light.
Ka_C01_S01_V13::block-0:
[Naciketas continues:] — Such-qualified being the heavenly realm, the means of attaining it is the Fire (Agni); that Agni, svargyam, leading to heaven, sa tvam, you, O Mṛtyu, adhyeṣi, you study, recall, that is, you know — this is the meaning. He Mṛtyo, since you know it, prabrūhi, declare, expound it, śraddadhānāya mahyam, to me who am full of faith and desirous of heaven.

That very Fire, by whose ritual piling, the sacrificers — those for whom the heavenly world is their goal, svarga-lokāḥ — bhajante, attain amṛtatvam, deathlessness, that is the state of the gods; that knowledge of the Fire, etat agni-vijñānam, dvitīyena vareṇa vṛṇe, I crave by the second boon.
Ka_C01_S01_V14::block-0:
This is Mṛtyu's promise: — te tubhyam prabravīmi, I declare unto you what you have asked; tat u me nibodha, do you, with one-pointed mind, attentively hearken to my speech. Svargyam, conducive to heaven and the means thereof, that Agni, he Naciketas — prajānan, I being indeed one who knows it well, this is the sense. The phrases 'I shall declare it' and 'do you mark it' are uttered to settle and compose the disciple's mind.

Now he extols that Fire: — anantalokāptim, the means of attaining the fruit consisting in the world of heaven; atho, and also pratiṣṭhām, the support of the universe in the form of Virāj; tam etam, this very Agni about to be expounded by me, viddhi, know, niveśitam, abiding, guhāyām, in the cave — that is, established in the intellect of the wise.
Ka_C01_S01_V15::block-0:
This is the speech of Śruti: — lokādim, the first among the worlds, since it is the first being to assume embodiment; that very Agni, the topic in hand, sought by Naciketas, uvāca, he, Mṛtyu, declared tasmai, to that Naciketas. Furthermore, the bricks (iṣṭakāḥ) that are to be heaped, in their proper form; yāvatīḥ, of what number; yathā vā, and in what manner the Fire is to be ritually piled — all this he expounded; this is the sense.

And Naciketas too, with apt comprehension, repeated back word for word what was thus declared by Mṛtyu — pratyavadat, he uttered it again exactly. Then, gratified by his repetition, Mṛtyu, tuṣṭaḥ, well-pleased, punar evāha, addressed him once more, intending to bestow yet another boon over and above the three already promised.
Ka_C01_S01_V16: Greatly pleased, the noble-souled one said to him: 'I grant you here today yet a further boon. This fire shall be known by your very name. And take this many-formed garland.'
Ka_C01_S01_V16::block-0:
How (was this said)? He said to him, to Naciketas — being pleased (prīyamāṇaḥ), that is, beholding the fitness of the disciple and experiencing delight; the great-souled one (mahātmā), that is, one of non-petty intellect, said: 'I now, today (adya), grant you (dadāmi bhūyaḥ) yet a further fourth boon here, on account of my satisfaction — I bestow it again.'

'This fire of which I have been speaking shall become well-known by your very name, that is, by the name of Naciketas (tavaiva nāmnā).' Moreover: 'Take, accept this garland (sṛṅkām) — sonorous, made of jewels, this many-formed (anekarūpām), variegated one.' Or alternatively, 'Take this sṛṅkā — that is, the unblamable course consisting of action (karma).' The meaning is: 'Accept also the other thing — the knowledge of works — since it is the cause of manifold fruits.'
Ka_C01_S01_V17: He who, having met the threefold connection, performs the Nāciketa fire thrice and does the threefold action, crosses beyond birth and death. Knowing the adorable god, born of Brahmā, the omniscient one, and realising him (as the Self), he attains this peace absolutely.
Ka_C01_S01_V17::block-0:
Once again he proclaims the praise of action — Triṇāciketas: he by whom the Nāciketa fire has been kindled three times is Triṇāciketas; or, one who possesses knowledge of it. 'Having reached (etya) the connection (sandhi) — that is, having received proper instruction — through the three (tribhiḥ): mother, father, and teacher.' That this is the cause of authority is gathered from another scriptural passage: 'just as one having a mother, having a father (yathā mātṛmān pitṛmān)' (Bṛ. U. 4.1.2) and so forth. Or alternatively, by the three — namely, those approved by Veda and Smṛti, or by perception, inference, and scripture. From these, indeed, comes purification, evidently so.

Trikarmakṛt — the doer of the three works: sacrifice (ijyā), study (adhyayana), and gift (dāna) — crosses beyond birth and death. Moreover: Brahmajajña — born of Brahman (Hiraṇyagarbha) is brahmaja; he is brahmaja and also jña (knower); for he is omniscient. Him, the deva — luminous, endowed with knowledge and other qualities — the īḍya (worthy of praise), having known (viditvā) through scripture, having beheld (nicāyya) (him) as one's own Self, one attains this supreme peace (śānti) — the cessation directly perceived in one's own intellect — in the highest measure. The meaning is: by the conjoint practice of knowledge and works, one attains the station of Virāj.
Ka_C01_S01_V18: He who, knowing these three, being thus a knower, performs the Nāciketa fire as Triṇāciketas, casting away beforehand the snares of death, transcending sorrow, rejoices in the world of heaven.
Ka_C01_S01_V18::block-0:
Now he concludes the fruit of the knowledge and the kindling of the fire, and also (the conclusion of) the topic — Triṇāciketas: 'having known (viditvā) these three (etat trayam) — namely, that which has been mentioned, viz. ‘what bricks, how many, and in what manner’ — and he who, knowing the fire thus as essentially identical with the Self (ātmasvarūpeṇa), performs the kindling — that is, accomplishes (nirvartayati) — the Nāciketa fire-sacrifice (kratu).'

'He, having pushed away beforehand (purataḥ praṇodya) — that is, before the fall of the body — the snares of death (mṛtyu-pāśān), characterised by adharma, ignorance, attachment, aversion, and the like; transcending sorrow (śokātigaḥ) — that is, freed from mental afflictions; rejoices (modate) in the heavenly world (svarga-loke), namely the realm of Virāj, by the realisation of his identity with the form of Virāj.'
Ka_C01_S01_V19: 'This fire of yours, O Naciketas, leading to heaven, which you chose with the second boon — this fire people will speak of by your very name. Choose now, O Naciketas, the third boon.'
Ka_C01_S01_V19::block-0:
'This (eṣaḥ) is your fire-boon, O Naciketas — leading to heaven (svargyaḥ), the means of attaining heaven — which fire-boon you chose, requested, with the second boon (dvitīyena vareṇa). That fire-boon has now been granted' — thus the conclusion of what was stated. Moreover: 'This fire (etam agnim) people (janāsaḥ — meaning ‘folk’) shall name (pravakṣyanti) by your own name.'

'This (further) boon, the fourth, has been given by me out of satisfaction. Now, O Naciketas, choose the third boon (tṛtīyaṃ varam).' The intended meaning is: 'Until that is given, I am, as it were, indebted.'
Ka_C01_S01_V20: 'There is this doubt regarding a man who is dead — some say He exists, while others say He does not. This I would know, instructed by you. Of all the boons, this is the third boon.'
Ka_C01_S01_V20::block-0:
From the foregoing scriptural matter — comprising injunctions and prohibitions through mantra and brāhmaṇa — it is to be understood that the matter indicated by the two (preceding) boons does not amount to the true cognition of the reality of the Self (ātma-tattva-yāthātmya-vijñāna). Hence, in order to remove the natural ignorance (avidyā) — which is the seed of saṃsāra and consists in the superimposition (adhyāropaṇa) of action, agent, and fruit upon the Self — by means of its opposite, namely the cognition of the unity of Brahman and the Self (brahma-ātma-aikatva-vijñāna), which is devoid of the superimposition of action, agent, and fruit and which has supreme liberation (ātyantika-niḥśreyasa) for its purpose — that knowledge must now be expounded; hence the subsequent text begins.

This very subject he expounds through narrative — showing that even with the attainment of the second boon, fulfilment is not yet reached without that knowledge of the Self which is the province of the third boon. And since the eligibility (adhikāra) for the knowledge of the Self belongs only to one who has become dispassionate towards what is non-eternal — the realm of works characterised by means and ends, dealt with previously — therefore, in order to censure (those works), the temptation is offered through the mention of sons and the like.

Naciketas spoke (when told 'O Naciketas, choose the third boon'): 'Whatever is this doubt (vicikitsā) regarding a man who has departed (prete) — some hold that there is (asti) a Self, distinct from body, senses, mind, and intellect, related to another body; while others hold that no such Self exists. Here we have no certain knowledge either by direct perception or by inference. And the supreme human end depends on this knowledge. Therefore, this I would learn, being instructed (anuśiṣṭaḥ) — that is, made to know — by you. This is the third, the remaining, boon among my boons.'
Ka_C01_S01_V21: 'Even by the gods of old this matter has been doubted; for it is not easily known — subtle indeed is this dharma. Choose, O Naciketas, another boon. Do not press me; release me from this.'
Ka_C01_S01_V21::block-0:
In order to test whether he is decisively fit for the knowledge of the Self that is the means of supreme good, or not, he says: 'Even by the gods (devaiḥ api), in former times (purā), in this very matter (atra), there has been doubt (vicikitsitam). For it is not easily knowable (na hi suvijñeyam) — that is, not well-cognised even when heard repeatedly — by ordinary persons; since this dharma called the Self is subtle (aṇuḥ — sūkṣmaḥ).'

'Therefore, O Naciketas, choose another boon (anyaṃ varam) — one whose fruit is undoubted. Do not obstruct (mā mā uparotsīḥ) me — make no obstruction, as a creditor towards a debtor. Release (atisṛja — vimuñca), let go of this boon — release me from it.'
Ka_C01_S01_V22: 'Even by the gods, indeed, this matter has been doubted; and you yourself, O Death, say it is not easily knowable. Yet a teacher of this like you cannot otherwise be found, and no other boon equal to this exists.'
Ka_C01_S01_V22::block-0:
Thus addressed, Naciketas says: 'It has been doubted by the gods even in this matter, indeed (kila) — so we have heard from yourself. And you, O Death (mṛtyo), say (āttha) that this reality of the Self is not easily knowable (na sujñeyam). Hence, since it is unknowable even by the learned, an expounder of this dharma like you (tvādṛk) — your equal — cannot otherwise be found, even by searching.'

'But this boon is the cause of attaining supreme good. Therefore, no other boon equal (tulyaḥ — sadṛśaḥ) to this exists. The intended sense is: because all other (boons) yield only non-eternal fruit.'
Ka_C01_S01_V23: 'Choose sons and grandsons living a hundred years, abundant cattle, elephants, gold, and horses; choose a vast tract of the earth as your domain, and you yourself live for as many autumns as you wish.'
Ka_C01_S01_V23::block-0:
Even thus addressed, Death again, tempting (Naciketas), said: 'Choose sons and grandsons (putra-pautrān) living a hundred years (śatāyuṣaḥ) — those whose lifetimes are a hundred years. Moreover, many cattle (bahūn paśūn) — namely, of the kind beginning with cows — and elephants and gold (hasti-hiraṇyam — meaning ‘elephant and gold’), and horses.'

'Moreover, choose a great (mahat — vast) territory (āyatanam — domain, region, sovereign empire) of the earth (bhūmeḥ — pṛthivyāḥ).' Further, since all this would be useless if one's own life were brief, he says: 'And you yourself, live (jīva) — sustain the body together with all the senses — for as many autumns (śaradaḥ — years) as you wish to live.'
Ka_C01_S01_V24: ‘If you regard any boon as equal to this one, choose it; choose wealth and long life as well. O Naciketas, become the ruler over the vast earth. I make you the enjoyer of all desires.’
Ka_C01_S01_V24::block-0: ‘Equal to this’ — that is, equivalent to the boon already taught (the knowledge of the fire-sacrifice). If you consider any other boon as equal to this, then choose that as well. Furthermore, choose abundant wealth — gold, jewels and the like — together with long life; this is the import. What more need be said? On the great earth — that is, in the vast realm — be a king, O Naciketas; become such a one. And further: of desires both divine and human, I make you the partaker (kāmabhāj), the legitimate enjoyer, one entitled to all desires; for I am a god whose resolve is unfailingly true (satyasaṅkalpa).
Ka_C01_S01_V25: ‘Whatever desires are hard to win in the world of mortals — ask for all those desires according to your will. Here are these maidens with their chariots and music; such ones are not to be won by men. Be served by these whom I bestow upon you. O Naciketas, do not ask about death.’
Ka_C01_S01_V25::block-0: Whatever desires are coveted yet unattainable (durlabha) in the world of mortals — ask for all of them according to your wish (chandataḥ). And further: these are divine apsaras-women — they are called rāmā because they delight men, sarathā because they come together with chariots, satūryā because they are accompanied by musical instruments. Such women, of this very kind, are not to be obtained by mortals like you without the grace of one such as me. By these whom I bestow — these handmaidens given by me — have your service performed: have your feet washed and the like attendance rendered upon yourself; this is the meaning. O Naciketas, do not press further with your question concerning death — that question of the form ‘does it exist after departing the body or not?’, which is like investigating the teeth of a crow (a useless inquiry); you ought not to ask in this manner.
Ka_C01_S01_V26: ‘O Ender, the morrow-things of mortals wear away the vigour of all the senses. Even the whole of life is little. Let the chariots remain yours, yours the song and dance.’
Ka_C01_S01_V26::block-0: Naciketas, though thus tempted by Death, remained unshaken like a deep lake, and replied — ‘śvobhāva’ means: those of which the very being or arising tomorrow remains doubtful, ‘will it be or will it not be?’ — the enjoyments you have just placed before me. And further: O Ender, O Death, of the mortal — of man — what vigour belongs to all the senses, that they (these so-called pleasures) wear down and exhaust. The pleasures beginning with the apsarases lead only to harm, since they sap dharma, virility, wisdom, lustre, fame and the rest. As for the long life you wish to grant — hear this too: the whole life-span, even of Brahmā, is itself but little; how much more so the long life of the likes of us! Therefore let your chariots and the rest abide with you alone, and so too your song and dance.
Ka_C01_S01_V27: ‘A man cannot be satisfied by wealth. Shall we acquire wealth when we have looked upon you? We shall live only so long as you ordain. The boon I would choose is that one alone.’
Ka_C01_S01_V27::block-0: Further: a man cannot be made content even by abundant wealth. Nowhere in the world is the gain of wealth seen to confer satisfaction on anyone. Even granting that we did have a thirst for wealth — we shall obtain (lapsyāmahe) wealth, since we have beheld (adrākṣma) you. The case of life is just the same — we shall live only so long as you, in the realm of Yama, will rule, will be the lord. For how, having met you, can a mortal remain of meagre wealth or short life? But the boon I have to choose is that one alone — namely, the knowledge of the Self (ātma-vijñāna).
Ka_C01_S01_V28: ‘What decaying mortal, dwelling here below upon the earth, having approached the undecaying immortals and recognising (something higher) from them, would delight in long life when he reflects on the pleasures of beauty, love and joy?’
Ka_C01_S01_V28::block-0:
Since, having approached (upetya) the undecaying ones — those who do not undergo decline of age, the immortals — and learning from them that there is some higher purpose for the Self yet to be attained, knowing this and yet himself decaying — a mortal subject to old age and death — and ‘kvadhaḥsthaḥ’: ‘ku’ means earth, which lies below in relation to the heavens and the rest, and he who stands upon it is ‘kvadhaḥsthaḥ’ — being thus, how would such a one ask for what only the undiscriminating crave: unstable son, wealth and the rest? An alternative reading is ‘kva tadāsthaḥ’. On that reading the construal is this: he in whom there is firm clinging (āsthā), engagement with full intent, to those — sons, wealth and the like — is ‘tadāsthaḥ’. Eager to attain a far higher human goal, even though hard to win, where would he be one fixed on those (lower things)? — i.e., none who has known their hollowness would crave them; this is the meaning. For everyone in the world wishes to ascend higher and higher. Therefore I am not to be tempted by the lures of son, wealth and the like.

Moreover: discerning (abhidhyāyan) — examining as they really are — those pleasures of beauty, love and joy beginning with the apsarases, seeing them to be of unstable nature, what discerning man would delight in even an exceedingly long life?
Ka_C01_S01_V29: ‘O Death, that concerning which men entertain doubt — what arises in the great hereafter — tell us that. This boon, which has entered the deep, no other than this does Naciketas choose.’
Ka_C01_S01_V29::block-0: Therefore, having set aside the temptation by impermanent desires — that which I had asked for: O Death, regarding the one who has departed, where men entertain this doubt of the form ‘he is’ or ‘he is not’; in the great matter of the hereafter (sāmparāya), in this momentous concern, the certain knowledge of the Self — that, do tell us. What more need be said? This boon now under discussion, concerning the Self, which has reached and entered into what is hidden, deep and hard to discriminate — apart from that boon, no other boon, of the impermanent kind craved by the undiscerning, does Naciketas choose, not even in his mind. Such is the very utterance of the śruti.
Ka_C01_S02_V01: ‘The good (śreyas) is one, and the pleasant (preyas) quite another; the two, with differing aims, bind a man. Of the two, well does it fare with him who lays hold of the good; he falls away from the (true) end who chooses the pleasant.’
Ka_C01_S02_V01::block-0:
Having tested the disciple and ascertained his fitness for the vidyā, (Yama) speaks: śreyas — the highest good (niḥśreyasa) — is one thing, distinct in itself; and preyas — the more pleasing — is something else again. These two, śreyas and preyas, with differing aims, with separate ends, bind (sinītaḥ) the qualified person — the one marked by varṇa, āśrama and the rest. By these two — vidyā and avidyā — every man is impelled to act, taking each as something to be done by himself. For man engages in action wishing for prosperity (abhyudaya) and for immortality (amṛtatva), and these are the proper concerns of preyas and śreyas respectively. Hence every man is said to be bound by them, taking the ends of śreyas and preyas as his duty.

Though each of the two is connected with one or another human goal, since their forms are vidyā and avidyā they are mutually opposed; hence it is impossible for one and the same person to undertake both together without abandoning one. Therefore, of these two, abandoning preyas (which is of the form of avidyā), it goes well — auspiciously, blessedly — with him who takes up śreyas alone. But the short-sighted, deluded man falls away (hīyate) — is severed — from the (true) goal, the supreme, abiding human end. Who is this? — he who chooses (vṛṇīte) — takes up — preyas.
Ka_C01_S02_V02: ‘The good and the pleasant approach a man; the wise one, having gone round both, distinguishes them. The wise chooses the good in preference to the pleasant; the dull-witted chooses the pleasant for the sake of getting and keeping.’
Ka_C01_S02_V02::block-0:
If both are alike within a man's power to undertake, why does the world by and large lay hold only of preyas? — to this, the answer is given. True, both are within his power; yet, since for the dull-witted they are hard to discriminate as regards their means and their fruits, the two come to a man as if commingled. Therefore, like the swan separating milk from water, the wise one (dhīraḥ) — the discerning — having gone round (samparītya) both, śreyas and preyas, weighing their relative gravity in his mind, distinguishes them, sets them apart. Having so distinguished, he chooses śreyas alone in preference to preyas, since śreyas is the more worthy. Who is he? — the wise.

But he who is dull (mandaḥ) — of little understanding — being incapable of discriminating between the real and the unreal, chooses preyas — characterised by cattle, sons and the like — for the sake of yoga-kṣema, that is, for the sake of acquiring and preserving the body and its accessories.
Ka_C01_S02_V03: You, O Naciketas, having pondered upon objects dear to you and lovely in form, have cast them off. You have not accepted this wealth-laden path, in which many men sink.
Ka_C01_S02_V03::block-0:
‘That you, even though again and again tempted by me, were yet pondering upon (abhidhyāyan)’ — that is, reflecting upon — ‘the dear ones (priyān), namely sons and the like, and upon objects lovely in form (priyarūpān), namely the apsarases and so forth, considered as objects of desire (kāmān), discerning their faults of impermanence and unsubstantiality and the rest. O Naciketas, you have cast them off (atyasrākṣīḥ) — you have wholly relinquished and forsaken them. Ah, the depth of your discrimination!’

‘You have not accepted this contemptible path (sṛṅkām, sṛtim) — the way trodden by deluded folk — which consists of wealth (vittamayīm), where the bulk of it is mere riches; that path in which many (bahavaḥ), namely the multitude of the deluded (mūḍhāḥ), sink and come to grief.’ Thus Yama, beholding Naciketas’ readiness for śreyas and his renunciation of preyas, openly extols his discriminative wisdom.
Ka_C01_S02_V04: Far apart and divergent in their courses are these two — known as avidyā and vidyā. I deem you, Naciketas, a seeker of vidyā; the many objects of desire have not lured you away.
Ka_C01_S02_V04::block-0:
It has already been said: ‘Of these two, well does it fare with him who chooses śreyas; he forfeits the goal who chooses preyas’ (1.2.1). Why so? Because far apart (dūram) — that is, separated by a vast interval — are these two, mutually exclusive in their very nature: one consisting of discrimination and the other of non-discrimination, like darkness and light. Thus they are viṣūcī — moving in divergent directions, of different fruits, since one leads to saṃsāra and the other to liberation (mokṣa).

Which are these two? It is declared: avidyā, whose object is preyas, and vidyā, whose object is śreyas — thus known (jñātā), thoroughly ascertained (nirjñātā), comprehended by the wise. Among these two, you, O Naciketas, I deem (manye) a seeker of vidyā (vidyābhīpsinam) — one who longs for true knowledge.

Why so? Because the many desires (kāmāḥ) — apsarases and the like, which entice the intellect of the unwise — though numerous (bahavaḥ), have not lured you (nālolupanta) — they have not severed you from the path of śreyas by inducing in you the craving for self-enjoyment. Therefore I deem you a seeker of vidyā, a vessel fit for śreyas — such is the import.
Ka_C01_S02_V05: Dwelling in the midst of avidyā, deeming themselves wise and learned, the deluded go round and round, sorely buffeted, like blind men led by the blind.
Ka_C01_S02_V05::block-0:
But those who are tenants of saṃsāra, dwelling in the midst (antare) of avidyā — that is, swathed as if in a thick darkness, bound up by hundreds of cords of craving for sons, cattle, and the rest — yet themselves esteeming themselves to be wise (dhīrāḥ), endowed with discernment, and learned (paṇḍitāḥ), expert in the śāstras: these, going their crooked, manifold course (dandramyamāṇāḥ), running excessively to and fro, beset by the sorrows of old age, death, disease, and the rest, wander round (pariyanti).

The deluded (mūḍhāḥ), the undiscerning, are led by the very blind (andhenaiva) — by one bereft of sight — along a perilous path: just as in the world many blind men (bahavaḥ andhāḥ) following another blind guide come to great calamity, so do these. The likeness shows that the unwise teacher and the unwise pupil alike are doomed, since neither possesses the eye of discrimination.
Ka_C01_S02_V06: The means leading to the world beyond does not shine forth for the childish, careless, deluded by the infatuation of wealth. ‘This world alone is, there is no other’ — thinking thus, he falls again and again under my sway.
Ka_C01_S02_V06::block-0:
Hence, on account of this very delusion, sāmparāyaḥ does not become manifest. The world to which one is conducted (samparīyate) is sampar­āya — the world beyond; the special scriptural means (sādhanaviśeṣaḥ śāstrīyaḥ) directed towards its attainment is sāmparāya. That, towards a childish one (bālam) — an undiscerning man — does not shine forth (na pratibhāti), does not light up, does not draw near.

To whom (does it not shine)? To one who is heedless (pramādyantam) — committing pramāda, his mind clinging to objects such as sons, cattle, and the like; and likewise deluded by the infatuation of wealth (vittamohena) — one whose discrimination has been lost on account of riches, and is thus enveloped in tamas.

He, however, ever dwelling on the conviction, ‘This world alone (ayam eva lokaḥ), the visible one, distinguished by women, food, drink, and so on, is real; the other (paraḥ), the unseen world, is not (nāsti)’ — being thus a self-conceited believer (mānī) — repeatedly, being born again and again (punaḥ punaḥ janitvā), comes under the sway of mine — that is, of me, Death (mṛtyoḥ). The meaning is: he becomes mounted upon the unbroken chain of the sorrows characterised by birth, death, and the rest.
Ka_C01_S02_V07: He whom many do not even obtain for hearing, whom many even hearing do not know — wonderful is the speaker of him, skilled is the receiver of him; wonderful is the knower, instructed by one who is skilled.
Ka_C01_S02_V07::block-0:
For such, generally, is the world. But he who is a seeker of śreyas, he is found among thousands but as some one rare being who becomes a knower of the Self (ātmavid), of your kind. Why? Because for hearing (śravaṇāyāpi), even merely to hear of him, that Self is not obtained (na labhyaḥ) by many — by the multitude. And even hearing (śṛṇvanto’pi) — many others, hearing — yet do not know (na vidyuḥ), do not comprehend him; the unblest, those whose souls are unrefined, fail to discern.

Further, even the speaker (vaktā) of him is wonderful (āścaryaḥ), as a marvel: among many, scarcely one comes forth. Likewise, even of those who have heard, only some skilled one (kuśalaḥ) — fully expert — is the receiver (labdhā) of this Self; among many, hardly one. For the knower (jñātā) too is wonderful, scarcely one — even when instructed by one skilled (kuśalānuśiṣṭaḥ), that is, taught by a teacher who is himself adept and accomplished.

Thus a triple rarity is shown — rare is the teacher, rare is the disciple who attains, rarer still the knower; whence it is that this knowledge of the Self is not the common possession of the unrefined.
Ka_C01_S02_V08: Declared by an inferior man, this Self is not well to be known, since he is variously thought upon. When proclaimed by one who is non-different, there is no further course (of doubt) here; for he is subtler than the subtle, beyond the reach of mere reasoning.
Ka_C01_S02_V08::block-0:
Why so? When declared (proktaḥ) by an inferior man (avareṇa nareṇa) — by one who is lowly, of merely worldly intellect — this Self, of whom you ask me, is not well, that is, thoroughly, knowable (suvijñeyaḥ): not capable of being thoroughly known. For he is variously (bahudhā) thought upon by disputants — as ‘he is’, ‘he is not’, ‘doer’, ‘non-doer’, ‘pure’, ‘impure’, and so on, in many ways.

How then is he well to be known? It is said: when proclaimed (prokte) by one non-different (ananyena) — by a teacher who beholds no separateness, who has himself become (in realisation) the Brahman-Self that is to be made known — concerning this Self, no course (gatiḥ) — that is, no further drift of speculation through the rounds of ‘he is’, ‘he is not’, and the like — remains here, in this Self; for the Self is of a nature wherein every alternative-mode (vikalpagati) has set: the Self transcends them all.

Or again: when the Self is proclaimed as non-different from one’s own self (svātmabhūte ananyasmin), here in this Self there is no other course of cognition (anyāvagatiḥ), since there is no other knowable thing apart from him. For this is the supreme consummation of knowledge — the realisation of the Self’s oneness. Hence, no further going (gantavyābhāva) remains here; nor any movement of saṃsāra remains here in the Self that has been proclaimed as non-different (ananye ātmani prokte), since liberation, the fruit of that knowledge, is its inseparable concomitant.

Or yet again: when the Self has been proclaimed by the teacher who has himself become the Brahman-Self that is being declared — proclaimed under non-difference — there is here no agatiḥ (failure of comprehension), no anavabodha, no aparijñāna. There does indeed arise that comprehension, having him for its object, in the hearer: ‘I am he, non-different from him, even as the teacher is.’ Such is the meaning. Thus is the Self well-knowable when proclaimed in this manner of non-difference by a teacher endowed with the āgama.

Otherwise (without such an ācārya), the Self comes to appear as something subtler (aṇīyān) than even the atomic measure (aṇupramāṇāt). He is then atarkyaḥ — not to be settled by mere reasoning; for if some atomic measure be assigned to him by reasoning, another, by his own surmising, will conjecture (the Self) as still subtler than that, and a third still subtler than that one. There is no terminus of reasoning anywhere. Therefore, the Self is to be known only through the words of a non-different teacher, not through unaided ratiocination — this strikes squarely against the tārkika and his school of self-fashioned hypotheses.
Ka_C01_S02_V09: This wisdom is not to be attained by reasoning; only when proclaimed by another it leads to true knowing, dearest one. You who have obtained it — ah, you are of true firmness! May we have a questioner like you, O Naciketas!
Ka_C01_S02_V09::block-0:
Therefore this conviction (matiḥ), born of the āgama, which has arisen in regard to the Self proclaimed under non-difference — this is not (na eṣā) by reasoning (tarkeṇa) — by mere conjecture of one’s own intellect — to be brought near (āpaneyā), that is, to be made attainable. Or (in another reading): not to be set aside (apaneyā), not to be overthrown.

For the tārkika, ignorant of the āgama, fashions only what his own private intellect has fancied, whatever it may be. Hence this very conviction, born of the āgama, when proclaimed (proktā) by another (anyena) — that is, by a teacher conversant with the āgama, distinct from a tārkika — becomes the means to genuine knowing (sujñānāya), O dearest one (preṣṭha), most beloved.

What then is this conviction, inaccessible to mere tarka? It is said: ‘the conviction which you (yām tvam) have obtained (āpaḥ), through the boon I bestowed.’ — One whose firmness (dhṛtiḥ) is true (satyā), having a non-deceptive object — that is, you, who are of true firmness (satyadhṛtiḥ).

‘Bata asi’ — ‘ah, indeed you are!’ — thus does Death speak with compassion to Naciketas, by way of the praise of the knowledge soon to be declared. ‘May one like you (tvādṛk), of your equal, become (bhūyāt) for us (naḥ).’ Let there be some other son or pupil who is a questioner (praṣṭā). Of what kind? Of the kind that you are, O Naciketas, the questioner.
Ka_C01_S02_V10: I know that the so-called treasure is impermanent, for the eternal is not attained by means of the impermanent. Yet by me the Nāciketa fire was kindled with impermanent things, and thereby I have attained that which is (relatively) eternal.
Ka_C01_S02_V10::block-0:
Pleased once again, Yama speaks. ‘I know (jānāmi aham) the treasure (śevadhiḥ) — the so-called nidhi, that which is sought after as one seeks a treasure, namely the fruit of works (karmaphalalakṣaṇaḥ). I know that this is impermanent (anityam, anityaḥ).’ For (na hi) by impermanent, fluctuating means (anityaiḥ adhruvaiḥ) is that which is permanent (nityam) and steadfast (dhruvam) — the supreme-Self-named treasure (paramātmākhyaḥ śevadhiḥ) — to be attained.

But that treasure which has the nature of impermanent happiness (anityasukhātmakaḥ śevadhiḥ) — that indeed is attained by impermanent things (anityair dravyaiḥ prāpyate hi). Therefore (tataḥ), even though I knew this — that the eternal cannot be reached by impermanent means — yet by me the Nāciketa fire was kindled (cita): the fire that is the means to heavenly happiness was set up using impermanent substances such as cattle and the like. By that, I, having attained eligibility (adhikāra), have reached (prāptavān asmi) the place of mine, which is here named svarga — eternal in a relative sense (āpekṣikam nityam) only.

The meaning is: of the truly eternal Brahman-treasure, no impermanent ritual is the producer; yet for that relative permanence which men call ‘heaven’, kindled rites avail. Thus does Yama implicitly distinguish the fruit of karma from the fruit of vidyā, preparing the ground for the higher teaching of śreyas.
Ka_C01_S02_V11: Having beheld the fulfilment of all desire, the foundation of the world, the endless fruit of sacrificial rite, the further shore of fearlessness, the great and far-reaching seat worthy of praise, the supreme abode — yet, O wise Naciketas, you with steadfast resolve renounced it all.
Ka_C01_S02_V12: That ancient Self, hard to behold, hidden, having entered within, lodged in the cave of the heart, dwelling in the depth — the wise man, by realising it through the yoga of inward meditation, abandons both joy and sorrow.
Ka_C01_S02_V12::block-0:
That Self which you wish to know — He is durdarśa, hard to behold, since on account of His extreme subtlety it is difficult to perceive Him; gūḍha, hidden, profound; anupraviṣṭa, having entered within, that is, concealed by the cognitions pertaining to ordinary objects.

He is guhāhita, lodged in the cave, that is, set in the buddhi (intellect), placed and abiding there, because He is apprehended therein. Gahvareṣṭha — He stands in the gahvara, in the rugged terrain hemmed in by manifold afflictions; hence gahvareṣṭha. Just because He is hidden, has entered within, and is lodged in the cave, He is therefore gahvareṣṭha; and for that very reason He is hard to behold.

That puruṣa, the ancient one, knowing through adhyātma-yoga — withdrawing the mind from sense-objects and fixing it on the Self is adhyātma-yoga; its adhigama, attainment, by means of that — having known the Self as God, the wise man (dhīra) abandons joy and sorrow, since for the Self there is neither exaltation nor depression.
Ka_C01_S02_V13: Having heard this, having grasped it well, having drawn forth the righteous, having attained this subtle Self — the mortal rejoices, for he has obtained that which is worthy of rejoicing. I deem the abode flung wide open for Naciketas.
Ka_C01_S02_V13::block-0:
Moreover, this truth of the Self which I shall now declare — having heard it from the teacher, and having well taken it up, fully embraced it as one's own Self, the mortal — that is, one subject to death — having drawn it forth, raising it up, separating it from the body and the rest, and having attained this subtle Self that does not depart from dharma (dharmya), that mortal, the knower, rejoices, having obtained the Self which is verily worthy of rejoicing, the source of all gladness.

This Brahman, of such a nature, is the sadma, the abode; and I deem the door of that abode to be flung open, turned towards Naciketas, that is, towards you. The intent is: I deem you fit for liberation.
Ka_C01_S02_V14: That which is other than dharma and other than adharma, other than this caused-and-cause, other than the past and the future — that which you see, tell me that.
Ka_C01_S02_V14::block-0:
Having heard this, Naciketas spoke again: If I am worthy, and if you, Bhagavan, are pleased with me — then teach me that which is other than dharma, that is, other than the scriptural performance of duty, its fruit, and its instruments — distinct from all these, this is the meaning.

Likewise other than adharma, the sin which consists in the omission of enjoined acts; and other than this kṛta-akṛta — the kṛta is the effect, the akṛta is the cause: other than these. Further, other than the bhūta, the past time, and the bhavya, the future, and likewise other than the present. The meaning is: that which is not delimited by the three times.

If you behold, that is, know, such a reality which lies beyond the range of all empirical usage, declare that to me.
Ka_C01_S02_V15: That station which all the Vedas proclaim, which all austerities declare, desiring which men live the life of brahmacarya — that station I tell you in brief: it is this — Om.
Ka_C01_S02_V16: This syllable indeed is Brahman; this syllable indeed is the Supreme. Knowing this very syllable, whatever one desires, that becomes his.
Ka_C01_S02_V16::block-0:
Hence, this very syllable (Om) is Brahman, the lower (apara); and this very syllable is also the Supreme (para). For of both, this syllable is the symbol (pratīka). Knowing this very syllable, that is, worshipping it as Brahman, whoever desires whatever — whether the higher or the lower — that becomes his.

If the higher, it is to be known; if the lower, it is to be attained.
Ka_C01_S02_V17: This support is the highest; this support is the supreme. Knowing this support, one is glorified in the world of Brahman.
Ka_C01_S02_V17::block-0:
Since this is so, therefore this very Om is, of all supports for the attainment of Brahman, the most excellent, the most praiseworthy. This support is both the supreme and the lower, since it has both the higher and the lower Brahman as its scope.

Knowing this support, one is glorified in the world of Brahman. The meaning is: in the supreme Brahman and in the lower Brahman alike, having become Brahman, one becomes worthy of worship like Brahman itself.
Ka_C01_S02_V18: The wise Self is not born, nor does it die; it has not come from anywhere, nor has anything come from it. Unborn, eternal, everlasting, ancient — it is not slain when the body is slain.
Ka_C01_S02_V18::block-0:
By the words 'other than dharma' and so on, the Self that was inquired about, devoid of every distinction, has been pointed out — by means of Om as its support and as its symbol — and so also the lower Brahman, for the sake of the dull and the middling. Now, however, with the desire to determine the very nature of that Self of which Om is the support, this is being said.

It is not born, does not come into being; nor does it die — it is not subject to death. The many modifications of an originated, non-eternal thing have, as their first and last, the modifications of the form of birth and destruction. These two are first negated of the Self in order to deny all modifications: 'is not born, nor does it die'.

Vipaścit — wise, intelligent — because its nature, consciousness, is never broken or interrupted. Further, this Self has not come into being from any cause whatsoever; nor has anything else, distinct from it, come into being from this Self. Hence, this Self is unborn, eternal, everlasting, free from decay.

For that which is non-everlasting decays; but this is everlasting, and for that very reason ancient — that is, even though existing from of old, it is ever new. For that which is brought into being by the accretion of parts is now new — like a wall and the like; but the Self, opposite to that, is ancient, free from growth — this is the meaning.

Since this is so, therefore it is not slain, not injured, when the body is slain by weapons and the like; though abiding within it, like space.
Ka_C01_S02_V19: If the slayer think to slay, and if the slain think himself slain, both these fail to know; this neither slays nor is slain.
Ka_C01_S02_V19::block-0:
Even though the Self is of such a nature as has just been described, one whose vision of the Self is confined to the body alone — if such a man, the slayer (hantā), thinks (manyate), that is, considers, intends, "I shall slay him," wishing to slay (hantum); and likewise the other, who is the slain, also (cet), if he thinks (manyate) the slain Self, namely, "I have been slain" — both these (ubhau) do not know (na vijānītaḥ) their own Self truly. For this Self does not slay (na ayaṃ hanti), since the Ātman is changeless (avikriyatvāt); and likewise it is not slain (na hanyate), being changeless like ākāśa (space) for that very same reason.

Hence transempirical existence (saṃsāra), characterised by dharma and adharma and the rest, belongs only to the domain of one ignorant of the Self (anātmajña-viṣaya), not to the knower of the Self (ātmajña). For both by the authority of śruti (śruti-prāmāṇyāt) and by reasoning (nyāyāt), the applicability of dharma and adharma to the knower stands refuted (anupapatteḥ). Thus Śaṅkara fixes that mokṣa rests upon vidyā alone, and the entire saṃsāric machinery of agency and fruit operates only where adhyāsa upon the Self has not been dispelled.
Ka_C01_S02_V20: Subtler than the subtle, greater than the great, the Self is set in the cavity of the heart of every creature. One free from desire, with sorrow gone, beholds Him — that majesty of the Self — through the calming of the senses, by the grace of the Creator.
Ka_C01_S02_V20::block-0:
How then does one come to know the Self? It is now told. Subtler (aṇīyān) than the subtle (aṇoḥ), that is, more minute than even the śyāmāka grain and the like; and greater (mahīyān) than the great (mahataḥ), that is, of greater magnitude than the earth and the like. Whatever object — minute or vast — exists in the world, exists only because of this eternal Self pervading it as its very being (ātmavat sambhavati). Disjoined from that Self, it would lapse into the unreal (asat-sampadyate). Hence this very Self is subtler than the subtle and greater than the great, since it is conditioned by all upādhis of name and form (sarva-nāma-rūpa-vastu-upādhikatvāt).

And that Self of this creature — of the whole class of beings extending from Brahmā down to a tuft of grass (brahmādi-stamba-paryanta) — stands lodged (nihitaḥ) in the cavity (guhāyām), that is, in the heart, as their very inmost being (ātmabhūtaḥ sthitaḥ). Him, the Self, marked by the signs of seeing, hearing, reflecting and knowing (darśana-śravaṇa-manana-vijñāna-liṅgam), one who is akratuḥ — desireless (akāmaḥ), that is, whose buddhi has withdrawn from outer objects, both seen and unseen (dṛṣṭa-adṛṣṭa-bāhya-viṣayebhyaḥ uparata-buddhiḥ) — beholds.

When this withdrawal occurs, the instruments such as manas — the dhātus, so called because they uphold (dhāraṇāt) the body — grow tranquil (prasīdanti); and through this prasāda of the dhātus he beholds the majesty (mahimānam) of the Ātman, free from increase and decrease wrought by karman (karma-nimitta-vṛddhi-kṣaya-rahitam), realising directly, "This very one I am" (ayam aham asmi). Thereby he becomes free of sorrow (vigata-śokaḥ).
Ka_C01_S02_V21: Sitting He travels far; lying He goes everywhere. Who but I is fit to know that god, exulting and not exulting?
Ka_C01_S02_V21::block-0:
Otherwise this Self is hard to know (durvijñeya) for kāmins, for ordinary persons (prākṛta-puruṣaiḥ) — since, while seated (āsīnaḥ), abiding and motionless indeed, He travels far (dūraṃ vrajati), and while lying (śayānaḥ) He goes everywhere (sarvataḥ yāti). Thus this Self, the Deva, is mada-amada — both with exultation and without (samadaḥ ca amadaḥ ca, saharṣaḥ ca aharṣaḥ ca) — bearing seemingly contradictory attributes (viruddha-dharma-vān). Therefore being impossible to grasp, who, other than one like myself, is fit to know that mada-amada Deva (kaḥ taṃ mad-amadaṃ devaṃ mad-anyaḥ jñātum arhati)?

For only one like ourselves, a paṇḍita of subtle intellect (sūkṣma-buddhi), can know this Self. Being conditioned by many mutually contradictory attributes such as stasis and motion, eternality and non-eternality (sthiti-gati-nitya-anitya-ādi-viruddha-aneka-dharma-upādhikatvāt), the Self appears manifold like the universal form (viśva-rūpa iva), or like the cintāmaṇi gem to one or another beholder. Hence the difficulty of knowing is shown — "Who other than me is fit to know him?" Lying (śayanam) is the cessation (upaśama) of the karaṇas; in the sleeper, the partial cognition (eka-deśa-vijñāna) born of the karaṇas comes to rest. When this is so, since only the universal cognition (kevala-sāmānya-vijñāna) remains, He as it were goes everywhere (sarvato yāti iva). When set in particular cognition (viśeṣa-vijñāna-sthaḥ), abiding indeed in His own form, yet on account of being conditioned by the movements of manas and the rest, He as it were travels far (dūraṃ vrajati iva). Yet truly He stands here itself (ihaiva vartate).
Ka_C01_S02_V22: Knowing the Self as bodiless among bodies, as steady among the unsteady, as great and all-pervading, the wise man does not grieve.
Ka_C01_S02_V22::block-0:
By the knowledge of that Self the cessation of grief (śoka-atyaya) ensues; this too is shown. Aśarīraḥ — by His own nature like ākāśa (svena rūpeṇa ākāśa-kalpaḥ), the Ātman is bodiless. Him — the bodiless one — set in the bodies (śarīreṣu) of devas, pitṛs, men and the rest, which are themselves anavastheṣu — devoid of fixed standing, that is, non-eternal (anityeṣu) — yet abiding (avasthitam) eternal and unaltered (nityam avikṛtam), this is the import.

Mahāntam — great. Lest greatness be supposed to be merely relative (mahattvasya āpekṣikatva-śaṅkāyām), it is said: vibhum, all-pervading (vyāpinam), the Ātman. The grasping by the word ātmā is to indicate that He is not other than oneself (svataḥ ananyatva-pradarśanārtham). The word "ātman" refers principally to the inmost Self (pratyag-ātma-viṣaya eva mukhyaḥ).

Knowing such an Ātman as "This I am" (ayam aham iti), the dhīraḥ — the wise — does not grieve. For grief is impossible (śoka-anupapatti) for one who has thus realised his own Self.
Ka_C01_S02_V23: This Self is not to be attained by exposition, nor by intellect, nor by much hearing. Whom this Self chooses, by him alone is It attained: to him this Self reveals Its own form.
Ka_C01_S02_V23::block-0:
Although this Self is hard to know, yet by a means He becomes well-knowable (su-vijñeya); thus it is said. This Self is not (na ayam ātmā) attained by pravacana — by the appropriating to oneself of many Vedas (aneka-veda-svīkaraṇena), that is, not knowable thus; nor by medhā — the power of grasping and retaining the meaning of texts (grantha-artha-dhāraṇa-śaktyā); nor by bahunā śrutena — by mere broad learning (bāhuśrutyena kevalena).

By what then is He attained? It is told — Whom (yam eva) this very seeker (eṣa sādhakaḥ) — i.e., one's own Self — chooses (vṛṇute), prays for (prārthayate), by that very Self as the chooser (varitrā), the Self Himself is attained (svayam ātmā labhyaḥ), that is, is known. The desireless one (niṣkāmaḥ) prays for the Self alone. The meaning is: the Self is attained by the Self itself (ātmanā eva ātmā labhyate).

How is He attained? It is told — to that one who longs for the Self (ātma-kāmasya), this Self reveals (vivṛṇute), discloses His own pāramārthikī tanu — the supremely-real form, that is, His own true essence (svakīyaṃ yāthātmyam). Thus Śaṅkara fixes that scholarship without longing for the Self bears no fruit; only the niṣkāma yearning for the Self draws forth the Self's self-disclosure.
Ka_C01_S02_V24: Not he who has not desisted from evil conduct, not he who is unrestrained, not he whose mind is unsettled, nor he whose mind is unstilled — none of these can attain Him, even by knowledge.
Ka_C01_S02_V24::block-0:
Further another point. One who has not desisted (na aviratah) from duścaritāt — from prohibited karma not enjoined by śruti and smṛti (pratiṣiddhāt śruti-smṛty-avihitāt pāpa-karmaṇaḥ), that is, has not turned away. Nor one who is unstilled (aśāntaḥ) from the wantonness of the indriyas (indriya-laulyāt), that is, not desisting. Nor the asamāhita — one of unfocussed mind (anekāgra-manāḥ), of distracted citta (vikṣipta-cittaḥ).

Even one of focused citta — for the sake of the fruit of samādhāna (samādhāna-phala-arthitvāt) — also not (nāpi) the aśānta-mānasaḥ, one whose citta is engaged in other concerns (vyāpṛta-cittaḥ vā). By prajñāna — by the knowledge of Brahman (brahma-vijñāna) — would attain Him (āpnuyāt), the Self under discussion (prakṛtam ātmānam).

But he who is desisted from evil conduct and from the wantonness of senses, of focussed citta, with mind quieted even from the fruit of samādhāna, possessed of an ācārya — by such prajñāna he reaches the Self as has been described — this is the meaning. Thus Śaṅkara enumerates the four-fold inner discipline that culminates in the śravaṇa-manana-nididhyāsana under a teacher; without these, mere knowledge does not arise.
Ka_C01_S02_V25: He for whom both Brāhmaṇa and Kṣatriya are food, and Death is the seasoning — who, except such a one, can know where He is?
Ka_C01_S02_V25::block-0:
But he who is not such — for whom that Self has Brahman and Kṣatra (brahma ca kṣatraṃ ca) — the brahma-kṣatra, upholders of all dharmas and the very life-breath of all beings (sarva-dharma-vidhārake api sarva-prāṇa-bhūte) — both as odana, as food (aśanam) — and Mṛtyu (mṛtyuḥ), who carries off all (sarva-haraḥ), as the upasecanam, like the seasoning to that food (upasecanam iva odanasya), and even so insufficient (aparyāptaḥ) for His meal — Him, with his prākṛta-buddhi, not addressed to the means previously stated (yathokta-sādhana-anabhiyuktaḥ san), who (kaḥ) ittham — thus, that is, as one possessed of those means (yathokta-sādhana-vān iva), can know (veda) where (yatra) that Self is?

Thus the impossibility of unqualified persons knowing Brahman, who consumes the entire universe of action and its fruit as His meal, is brought home; only the four-foldly disciplined sādhaka, addressed previously, has access. The grandeur of the Ātman is thus shown to require a corresponding inner equipment (adhikāra) in the seeker.
Ka_C01_S03_V01: Drinking the truth that is the fruit of action in the world of one's own good deeds, the two have entered the cavity, in the supreme abode of the Highest. The knowers of Brahman call them shadow and light, and so do those who maintain the five fires and have thrice kindled the Nāciketa fire.
Ka_C01_S03_V01::block-0:
The connection of this vallī beginning with "Ṛtaṃ pibantau" is this: vidyā and avidyā have already been set forth as having diverse and contradictory fruits (nānā-viruddha-phale), but those fruits have not yet been determined fully (na tu saphale te yathāvan nirṇīte). For settling these, the imagery of the chariot (ratha-rūpaka-kalpanā) is introduced, by which comprehension is rendered easier (pratipatti-saukaryam).

Accordingly, in order to discriminate prāptṛ (attainer), prāpya (the to-be-attained), gantṛ (goer), and gantavya (the destination) (prāptṛ-prāpya-gantṛ-gantavya-viveka-artham), through the chariot-imagery two ātmans are set forth — drinking ṛta, satya, the inevitable fruit of karman (avaśyaṃ-bhāvitvāt karma-phalam). Among the two, only one drinks the karma-phala — enjoys it (bhuṅkte) — not the other; nevertheless on account of association with the drinker they are spoken of as "both drinking" (pibantau iti ucyete) by the principle of "the umbrella-bearers" (chattri-nyāyena).

Sukṛtasya — of svayaṃ-kṛta karman; "ṛta" thus connects with the previous. Loke — in this body (asmin śarīre); guhām — into the cavity, the buddhi (buddhau praviṣṭau); parame — supreme, supreme in comparison with the spaces of the outer person (bāhya-puruṣa-ākāśa-saṃsthāna-apekṣayā paramam); parārdhe — the abode of the Highest, the Brahman, namely, the hṛd-ākāśa, the heart-space, for there itself the supreme Brahman is realised. Hence: "entered the supreme parārdha, the heart-space" — this is the import.

And these two are like chāyā and ātapa (chāyā-tapau iva) — distinguished by the marks of saṃsāritva and asaṃsāritva — so the brahma-vidaḥ, knowers of Brahman, declare. Nor only the akarmins declare it; the pañcāgnayaḥ — the householders (gṛhasthāḥ) — and those who are tri-nāciketāḥ — by whom thrice over the Nāciketa fire has been built up (triḥ-kṛtvaḥ nāciketo'gniḥ citaḥ yaiḥ te tri-nāciketāḥ) — also so declare. Thus Śaṅkara introduces the chariot-allegory as the methodological key to distinguishing pravṛtti and nivṛtti, the path of works and the path of knowledge.
Ka_C01_S03_V02: We are able to know the Nāciketa fire, which is like a bridge for sacrificers (the performers of rites), and that imperishable Brahman, the supreme refuge, which is fearless for those desirous of crossing to the further shore (of saṃsāra).
Ka_C01_S03_V02::block-0:
‘Yaḥ setuḥ’ — that which is like a bridge, hence a bridge — for ‘ījānānām’, that is, for sacrificers, the performers of rites; for it serves the purpose of crossing over sorrow. ‘Nāciketam’ — the Nāciketa fire — that we have been able to know and to kindle (cetum). Furthermore, that ‘abhayam’, fearless, the further shore of saṃsāra, which the knowers of Brahman desirous of crossing wish to attain — that supreme refuge, the imperishable Brahman known as the Self — that too may we be able to know.

The purport of the sentence is that the two Brahmans, the higher and the lower, which are the resorts respectively of the knowers of Brahman and of the performers of rites, are to be known; for indeed it is these two alone that have been introduced earlier in the passage ‘Ṛtaṃ pibantau’ (those two who drink the truth).
Ka_C01_S03_V03: Know the Self as the lord of the chariot, and the body indeed as the chariot. Know the intellect as the charioteer, and the mind as verily the reins.
Ka_C01_S03_V03::block-0:
Now then, for that transmigrating self which is constituted by the limiting adjuncts and is the one qualified by ignorance and knowledge, fit for going to liberation and to saṃsāra — for him a chariot is imagined as the means of travelling to either of those two destinations. Therein, ‘ātmānam’ — the saṃsārin who tastes the fruits — ‘know’ as the rathin, the lord of the chariot. ‘Know the body as verily the chariot’, since the body is dragged along by the senses, which stand in the place of the horses harnessed to the chariot.

‘But know the intellect, characterised by determination, as the charioteer’; for the body is principally guided by the intellect, just as a chariot is principally guided by the charioteer who steers it. Indeed, almost every action pertaining to the body is to be performed by the intellect. ‘And know the mind, characterised by volition and doubt and the like, as verily the reins (pragraha), the bridle.’ For the organs such as the ear, when held in by the mind, function — just as horses do when held by the reins.
Ka_C01_S03_V04: They call the senses the horses, and the objects (sense-fields) the paths trodden by them. The wise call the Self, conjoined with body, senses, and mind, the experiencer (enjoyer).
Ka_C01_S03_V04::block-0:
Those skilled in the imagery of the chariot ‘call’ the senses such as the eye ‘the horses’, on account of their common function of dragging the body-chariot. ‘Among them’, that is, among the senses figured as horses, ‘know’ the objects — forms and the rest — to be ‘gocarān’, the paths or roads. ‘Ātmendriyamanoyuktam’ — the Self conjoined and united with the body, the senses, and the mind — the wise discriminative ones ‘call the experiencer’, that is, the saṃsārin.

For the Self by itself has no experiencership; its experiencership is solely brought about by the limiting adjuncts of the intellect and so on. Accordingly, another Śruti also shows the non-experiencership of the Self alone — ‘He as it were thinks, He as it were trembles’ (Bṛ.U. 4.3.7) and so forth. This being so, by the imagery of the chariot to be set forth, the realisation of the Vaiṣṇava state as the very Self becomes intelligible, not otherwise, since it does not transgress its own real nature.
Ka_C01_S03_V05: Indeed, he who is without discrimination, with a mind always uncontrolled — his senses become unmanageable, like the wicked horses of a charioteer.
Ka_C01_S03_V05::block-0: This being so, ‘he who’ — that intellect-charioteer — ‘is avijñānavān’, unskilful, undiscerning regarding what is to be undertaken and what is to be avoided, just like another (mundane) charioteer in the conduct of the chariot, and is always conjoined with a mind that is ‘ayuktena’, ungrasped, unrestrained, uncomposed, mind which stands in the place of the reins — for that unskilful intellect-charioteer the senses, which stand in the place of the horses, become ‘avaśyāni’, impossible to restrain, like the wicked, untamed horses of an ordinary charioteer.
Ka_C01_S03_V06: But he who is endowed with discrimination, with a mind always controlled — his senses are obedient, like the well-trained horses of a charioteer.
Ka_C01_S03_V06::block-0: But, of him who is the charioteer of the opposite sort to that mentioned before, the result he states — ‘yastu vijñānavān’ — but he who is skilful, possessed of discrimination, always with a mind that is ‘yuktena’, restrained, with a composed mind — for him the senses, which stand in the place of the horses, are capable of being set going forth and being drawn back — they are ‘vaśyāni’, controlled, like the tamed, good horses (sadaśvāḥ) of another, expert charioteer.
Ka_C01_S03_V07: He who is without discrimination, mindless and ever impure — he does not attain that supreme abode, but reaches saṃsāra (the round of birth and death).
Ka_C01_S03_V07::block-0: Now, of the previously described intellect-charioteer who is undiscerning, this is the result that he states — ‘yastvavijñānavān bhavati’. He is ‘amanaskaḥ’, one whose mind is unrestrained; and being so, he is for that very reason always impure. That ‘rathin’ (lord of the chariot) does not, by means of that charioteer, attain ‘that’ supreme imperishable abode previously spoken of. Not only does he fail to attain it; he reaches saṃsāra characterised by birth and death.
Ka_C01_S03_V08: But he who is endowed with discrimination, with a controlled mind and ever pure — he attains that supreme abode whence he is not born again.
Ka_C01_S03_V08::block-0: But the second one, the rathin endowed with the discriminating charioteer, is ‘vijñānavān’ — that is to say, a man of knowledge (a vidvān). With a restrained mind, ‘samanaskaḥ’, he is, for that very reason, always pure. He alone attains ‘that abode’ — and once attained, not falling away from that abode, he is not again, ‘bhūyaḥ’, born in saṃsāra.
Ka_C01_S03_V09: But the man who has knowledge as his charioteer and holds the mind as the rein — he reaches the further shore of the road; that is the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
Ka_C01_S03_V09::block-0:
What is that abode? — to this he replies. ‘Vijñānasārathiḥ’ — he who, as before said, has the discriminating intellect as his charioteer; ‘manaḥpragrahavān’ — possessed of the mind as the reins, with a restrained mind, of composed inner instrument; being pure, the man of knowledge — ‘he attains the further shore of the road’, that is, of the way of saṃsāra, that very further shore which is to be reached; he is liberated from all the bonds of saṃsāra.

‘That’ is the supreme — most exalted — abode, place, of Viṣṇu, of the all-pervading Brahman, the supreme Self, named Vāsudeva — that is to say, His true essence (sat-tattva) — which the man of knowledge attains.
Ka_C01_S03_V10: Higher than the senses, indeed, are the objects (of the senses); higher than the objects is the manas; but higher than the manas is the buddhi; higher than the buddhi is the Mahat-Ātman.
Ka_C01_S03_V10::block-0:
Now, in order that the goal which is to be reached should be cognised in the order of progressive subtlety as the inmost Self, beginning from the gross senses, this passage is commenced. The senses, to begin with, are gross; higher than these senses, which are their (own) effects, are those higher objects (artha) by which, as the antecedent (causes), the senses have been produced for the manifestation of the Self — these objects are subtle, great, and inmost in nature. Higher than even these objects is the manas, which is subtler still, greater, and more inmost. By the word 'manas' is meant the subtle elemental substance which is the originator of the manas (-organ), since it is the originator of saṅkalpa, vikalpa, and the rest. Higher than the manas, again, is the buddhi — subtler still, greater still, and more inmost — the subtle elemental substance denoted by the word 'buddhi', which is the originator of adhyavasāya (determination) and so forth.

Higher than the buddhi is the Ātman — that is, the Mahat-Ātman, called so because it is the inmost Self of the buddhis of all living beings, and 'Mahat' (great) because of its greatness over all. That principle which is the first born from the Avyakta (Unmanifest), of the nature of Hairaṇyagarbha, partaking of both knowledge and non-knowledge — that Mahat-Ātman is here said to be higher than the buddhi.
Ka_C01_S03_V11: Higher than the Mahat is the Avyakta (Unmanifest); higher than the Avyakta is the Puruṣa; than the Puruṣa there is nothing higher: He is the culmination, He is the supreme Goal.
Ka_C01_S03_V11::block-0:
Higher than even the Mahat — subtler, more inmost in nature, and greater than all — is the Avyakta. It is the seed-principle of this entire universe, of the nature of unevolved name and form, the very essence consisting in the aggregate of all the powers of effects and causes — the Avyakta, denoted by such names as 'Avyākṛta' (the Unevolved), 'Ākāśa' (Ether), and the like, abiding in interpenetrative union (otaprota) with the Paramātman, even as the potency of the banyan tree resides in the banyan seed. Higher than that Avyakta is the Puruṣa — subtler still, since He is the cause of all causes, and 'Mahat' (great) because of being the inmost Self; and for that very reason He is 'Puruṣa', because He fills all (sarva-pūraṇāt).

Warding off the contingency of any other (entity) higher than Him, (the śruti) says, 'than the Puruṣa there is nothing higher.' Since there exists nothing whatsoever — no other reality — higher than the Puruṣa, who is a mere mass of consciousness (cinmātra-ghana), therefore He is the kāṣṭhā — the consummation, the final terminus — of subtlety, greatness and inmost-Selfhood. For here, beginning from the senses, the (gradation of) subtlety and the rest comes to its completion. And precisely for this reason, He is the supreme — i.e. the highest — goal of those that fare onward, of all the transmigrating beings who are wayfarers, in accordance with the smṛti, 'going whither, they return not' (Bh. Gītā 15.6).
Ka_C01_S03_V12: This Self, hidden in all beings, does not shine forth; but He is seen by the seers of the subtle, through the sharp and subtle buddhi.
Ka_C01_S03_V12::block-0:
Objection (pūrvapakṣa): If there is a 'going,' there must also be a 'coming back'; how then is it said, 'whence one is not born again' (Ka. Up. 1.3.8)? Answer: this is no defect. Since (the Puruṣa) is the inmost Self of all, the very avagati (cognition) is figuratively termed gati (going). And the inmost-Self-hood has been demonstrated by His being higher than the senses, manas, and buddhi. For he who 'goes' — goes towards a Puruṣa not of the inmost form, anātman in nature — he does not attain (Him) in His true essence. Thus also the śruti, 'pathless travellers, attaining the further shore in (apparent) paths' (?) and the like.

Thus it shows the inmost-Self-hood (with respect) to all: this Puruṣa, in all beings beginning with Brahmā down to a clump of grass, is gūḍha (concealed) — covered up — performing the activities of seeing, hearing, etc., veiled by the māyā of avidyā, and for that very reason the Ātman 'does not shine forth' as the Self of anyone. Ah! how very deep, hard to fathom, and wondrous indeed is this māyā, in that every creature, though in truth and reality possessed of the supreme essence, even when thus instructed, does not grasp 'I am the Paramātman'; while the non-Self — the aggregate of body, senses, etc., though seen as visible like a pot — he grasps as his Self, saying 'I am, I am the son of so-and-so,' even when not so told. Surely this whole world, deluded again and again by the māyā of the Supreme alone, wanders on bewildered. Thus also the smṛti — 'I am not manifest to all, being veiled by Yogamāyā' (Bh. Gītā 7.25) and so forth.

Objection: this is contradictory — that 'the wise man, knowing, grieves not,' and yet 'He does not shine forth.' Reply: not so. It has been said that He does not shine forth on account of His being incognisable to one whose buddhi is unrefined. But He is seen by the buddhi which has been refined and rendered agryā — sharpened to a point as it were, that is, made one-pointed (ekāgra); subtle, i.e. directed to the discernment of the subtle reality. By whom? By the sūkṣma-darśins — those whose habit it is to behold the supreme Subtle through perceiving the lineage of subtlety in the manner 'higher than the senses, indeed, are the objects' and so forth — by such seers of the subtle, that is, by the wise.
Ka_C01_S03_V13: Let the wise man restrain speech in manas; let him restrain that (manas) in the cognising Self (jñāna-ātman, i.e. buddhi); let him restrain knowledge (buddhi) in the Mahat-Ātman; let him restrain that in the peaceful Self.
Ka_C01_S03_V13::block-0:
(The śruti) states the means of attaining That: yacchet — let him restrain, draw in; the prājña, the discriminating one. What? vāc — speech; here 'speech' is upalakṣaṇa (an indicator) for all the senses. Where? manasi — in the manas; the long ī is a Vedic peculiarity (chāndasa). And let him restrain that manas in jñāna, that is, in the buddhi which is of the nature of light (prakāśa-svarūpa) — the Self (ātman). For the buddhi pervades the organs such as manas; thus it is their ātman and is the inmost (pratyak) for them.

Let him restrain jñāna — the buddhi — in the Mahat-Ātman, the Prathamaja (the First-born). The meaning is: let him render his own consciousness as transparent in nature (svaccha-svabhāva) as that of the Prathamaja. And let him restrain that Mahat-Ātman in the śānta — that Self in which all distinctions have set, who is unmodifying (avikriya), the inmost of all, the witness of every cognition of the buddhi, the principal, primary Ātman.
