Ka_C01_S03_V14: Arise! Awake! Having approached the excellent ones, learn (the Self); like the sharpened edge of a razor, hard to traverse — that path the wise declare difficult to tread.
Ka_C01_S03_V14::block-0:
Thus, when one has dissolved everything in the Puruṣa, the Ātman — the triad of nāma, rūpa, and karma, which is the unfurling of false knowledge (mithyājñāna), characterised as kriyā, kāraka and phala — by the very seeing of the true essence of one's own Self, just as the (apparent) water of a mirage, the snake on a rope, and the dirt on the sky (vanish) by the seeing of the true forms of the mirage, rope, and sky themselves — and one becomes self-poised, perfectly serene, with all duty done — therefore, for the sake of seeing That, (the śruti) addresses those asleep in beginningless avidyā: 'Arise! O creatures, turn your faces toward the knowledge of the Self! Awake! — make an end to that sleep of ignorance which is of dreadful form, the seed of all calamities.

 How? prāpya — having approached, drawing near to — varān — the most excellent, the knowers of the truth, the ācāryas; nibodhata — comprehend, that the Self taught by them, the inmost of all, is 'I am.' This must not be neglected, the śruti enjoins out of compassion, like a mother — because what is to be known is within the range of an exceedingly subtle buddhi.

What sort of subtleness of buddhi (is needed)? It is said: kṣurasya dhārā — the edge of a razor, niśitā — sharpened, made keen — duratyayā — that of which the traversing is hard, hence 'hard to cross.' Just as it is hard to walk over (a razor's edge) with the feet, so the path is durga — hard to accomplish, hard to attain. The kavayaḥ — the wise, the discerning — declare the path, that is, the path characterised as the knowledge of the truth (tattva-jñāna), to be such. The intent is: because what is to be known is exceedingly subtle, the path of knowledge that has it as its object is hard to accomplish.
Ka_C01_S03_V15: Soundless, touchless, formless, undecaying — likewise tasteless, eternal, scentless — beginningless and endless, higher than the Mahat, fixed: discerning That, one is freed from the mouth of death.
Ka_C01_S03_V15::block-0:
How then is the exceeding subtleness of what is to be known (established)? It is explained. Gross indeed is this earth, packed with sound, touch, form, taste, and smell — the object of all the senses; and so likewise is the body. Therein, by the falling away of one quality at a time, of smell etc., is seen the gradation of subtlety, greatness, purity, eternality and the like in (the elements) beginning with water and ending in ākāśa. Where these gandha and the rest, all of them being modifications because of grossness, ending with sound (śabda), are not — what need is there to speak of (the Brahman's) unsurpassable subtlety and so forth? This the śruti shows: 'aśabdam, asparśam, arūpam, arasam, agandhavac ca yat' — that which is soundless, touchless, formless, tasteless, scentless. This Brahman has been (already) explained.

avyayam: that which possesses sound and so forth perishes (vyeti); but this, since it is devoid of sound and the rest, is avyaya — it does not perish, does not wane. For that very reason it is nityam (eternal); for that which perishes is anitya, while this does not perish — hence eternal. And eternal also for this reason: anādi — that of which there is no ādi, no cause, is anādi. That which has a beginning, being an effect, is anitya and dissolves into its cause, like earth and the rest; but this, being the cause of all, is non-effect, and being non-effect is eternal. There is no cause of It in which It might dissolve. So also anantam: that of which there is no anta, no effect, is anantam. As in the case of plantain and the like, even though their non-eternality is seen through the production of fruit and the like, yet so is it not (the case) with Brahman; therefore also is It eternal.

mahataḥ param — higher than the Mahat principle called buddhi, distinguished from it because of being of the nature of eternal cognition (nitya-vijñapti-svarūpa); for Brahman is the witness of all, being the Self of all beings. As has been said, 'eṣa sarveṣu bhūteṣu' (Ka. Up. 1.3.12), and so on. dhruvam — and immutably steadfast (kūṭastha-nitya), not (merely) relative eternality such as belongs to earth and the rest. That Brahman, of such nature — the Ātman — having known (nicāya) Him as one's own Self, one is freed (pramucyate), separated from the mouth of mṛtyu, the domain of death characterised as avidyā, kāma, and karma.
Ka_C01_S03_V16: The wise man, having recited and heard this ancient Naciketas-narrative declared by Death, is exalted in the world of Brahman.
Ka_C01_S03_V16::block-0: In praise of the knowledge that has been expounded, the śruti says: nāciketam — that which has been attained by Naciketas, that is, naciketasā prāptam; mṛtyuproktam — declared by Mṛtyu — this ākhyāna or upākhyāna constituted by the three vallīs, sanātana — ancient, perpetual, because it is Vedic. Having uktvā (recited) it before brāhmaṇas, and having śrutvā (heard) it from ācāryas, the medhāvī — the man of penetrating intellect — brahmaiva loko brahmalokaḥ — Brahman alone is the loka, hence 'the Brahman-loka' — in that Brahmaloka mahīyate — is exalted, that is, becomes one with Brahman and the object of worship. This is the intent.
Ka_C01_S03_V17: Whoever, being self-restrained, recites this supreme secret in an assembly of Brāhmaṇas, or at the time of śrāddha — that (śrāddha) becomes capable of (yielding) infinitude. It becomes capable of infinitude. (Thus ends the chapter.)
Ka_C01_S03_V17::block-0: Whosoever should cause (others) to hear (śrāvayet) this granth — paramam, supreme, prakṛṣṭa, foremost, guhyam, the secret, what should be guarded — both as text and as meaning, in the assembly of brāhmaṇas, the brahma-saṃsad, prayataḥ, having become pure (śuci), or at the time of śrāddha — let him cause those eating (the śrāddha-meal) to hear (this) — that śrāddha kalpate — is rendered capable — of ānantya — infinite fruit. The repetition (of the phrase) marks the conclusion of the adhyāya.
Ka_C02_S01_INTRO1::block-0:
It has been declared, "This Self, hidden in all beings, is not manifest; yet it is seen by the keen and subtle buddhi" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.3.12). The natural question now arises: what then is the obstruction (pratibandha) to that subtle, one-pointed buddhi (agryā buddhi), through whose absence the Ātman fails to be seen? In order to display this very cause that prevents the seeing of the Self, the present valli is begun.

For when the cause obstructing śreyas (the supreme good) is once known, an effort can be undertaken to remove it; otherwise no such effort is even possible. Hence the order of teaching is reasonable: first the obstruction is exhibited, and only then the means for its removal can be enjoined.
Ka_C02_S01_V01: The Self-Existent (Svayambhū) bored the openings outward; therefore one looks outward, not at the inner Self. A certain wise man, desiring immortality, with eye turned inward, beheld the inmost Self.
Ka_C02_S01_V01::block-0:
Parāñci — "going outward," parāk añcanti gacchanti; khāni — the orifices, by which are indicated the senses such as the ear and the rest, called "openings" because the senses operate through them. They function only outward, parāñci eva, in order to manifest objects such as sound and the rest. Since their very nature is such, vyatṛṇat — He pierced, struck, did violence to them, the meaning being He fashioned them with this propensity. Who is this agent? Svayambhūḥ — the Supreme Lord, who is svayam eva svatantraḥ, self-existent, ever independent, never dependent on another.

Tasmāt — therefore parāṅ, outward, the perceiver perceives only the non-Self objects, sound and the rest, that have an outgoing form; na antarātman — not the inner Self; that is, he does not perceive the inner Ātman. Yet, even when the worldly course is thus naturally outward-turned, kaścit — some rare one, like the rare current that runs counter to the river's stream, dhīraḥ — possessed of dhī, of discrimination (viveka), beholds the pratyagātman. Pratyak ca asau ātmā ca iti pratyagātmā — he who is both "inward" and "Self" is the pratyagātman.

In ordinary usage the word ātman is established only in the inward-turned sense, not elsewhere. Even on the etymological side, the word ātman applies only to that very inward Self; for thus runs the smṛti on the derivation: "Because it pervades (āpnoti), because it appropriates (ādatte), because it experiences objects here (atti viṣayān iha), and because its being is uninterrupted (santato bhāvaḥ), therefore it is called ātman." That pratyagātman, his own true nature, aikṣat — he beheld; the meaning is, he beholds; in Vedic usage there is no fixed restriction of tense.

How does he behold? It is now told: āvṛttacakṣuḥ — one whose cakṣus, that is, the entire group of senses beginning with the ear, has been āvṛtta, turned back, withdrawn from the whole field of objects without remainder. Such a one, thus refined, beholds the pratyagātman; for it is impossible that one and the same person should be at once intent upon the contemplation of outer objects and engaged in the seeing of the inmost Self.

Desiring what does the dhīra take up this great labour, restraining the natural outward flow (svabhāva-pravṛtti-nirodha) and beholding the pratyagātman? It is told: amṛtatvam — the property of being deathless, the eternal nature, immortality of the Ātman — that is what he desires.
Ka_C02_S01_V02: The childish run after outward desires; they enter the wide-stretched noose of death. But the wise, knowing immortality as the fixed reality, ask not for any of these unstable things here.
Ka_C02_S01_V02::block-0:
What is by nature the perception that runs only outward, that is, the perception of non-Self — that is the obstructing cause to the seeing of the Self, namely avidyā. And contrary to it, lodged in those very outer fields shown forth by avidyā, is tṛṣṇā — thirst for the seen and unseen enjoyments. By these two — avidyā and tṛṣṇā — the seeing of the Self is held back. Therefore, parācaḥ — outward-going kāmān — desirable objects, the bālāḥ, the small-minded of slender prajñā, anuyanti — they go after; for that very reason they go to the pāśa, the noose, of mṛtyu — death, namely the aggregate of avidyā, kāma, and karma — vitatasya, of that which is widespread, pervading on every side, the noose characterized by the conjunction and disjunction of body and senses.

They unceasingly attain the manifold mass of evils — birth, death, old age, disease, and the rest. Since this is so, atha — therefore the dhīrāḥ — the discriminating, having known dhruvam — the fixed amṛtatvam, the immortality whose mark is abiding in the very nature of the pratyagātman. The immortality of the gods and the like is indeed adhruva — unfixed; but this, characterized by abiding in the very nature of the pratyagātman, is dhruva — fixed; for the śruti says, "It does not increase by action, nor become less."

Thus having ascertained that very kūṭastha, immovable, immortal nature, and having determined that all things, all states (padārtha), are adhruva — impermanent — the brāhmaṇas do not pray for anything whatever in this saṃsāra, abundant in evils, since all such things are antagonistic to the seeing of the pratyagātman. The drift of the passage is that they rise up entirely from the three eṣaṇās — desires for sons, wealth, and the worlds — and adopt nivṛtti, abandoning pravṛtti.
Ka_C02_S01_V03: Through which one knows form, taste, smell, sounds, touches, and the joys of union — through this very Self alone one knows them. What here remains beyond it? This indeed is That.
Ka_C02_S01_V03::block-0:
On knowing what is it that the brāhmaṇas no longer ask for anything else? How is its attainment? It is told: yena — by which Self, of the very nature of consciousness (vijñānasvabhāvena ātmanā), rūpam, rasam, gandham, śabdān, sparśān ca — and the maithunān, the cognitions of pleasure that arise from union — vijānāti — clearly knows; the whole world knows them.

Objection: such is not the world's prasiddhi, that "by an Ātman distinct from the body and the rest, I know." The whole world apprehends, on the contrary, "I, the body-aggregate, know."

Reply: not so. Since the body and the rest, being themselves of the nature of sound and so forth, are no different in this respect from objects, and since they are equally vijñeya — knowable — like other objects, vijñātṛtva — knowership — cannot reasonably belong to them. For if the body-aggregate, being itself rūpa-ādi-ātmaka, of the nature of form and the rest, were to know form and the rest, then external rūpādi too would mutually know each other and would know their own forms. But this is not seen.

Therefore, the rūpa-ādayaḥ, marked even with body and the rest, are known eteneva — by this very Self, distinct from body and the rest, of the nature of vijñāna. Just as one says "the iron burns," yet that by which the iron burns is fire — even so the world knows. And of the Ātman itself there is no other knower; the Ātman is not vijñeya, knowable as object.

Kim atra pariśiṣyate — what here, in this world, remains apart? Nothing remains; for everything is knowable through the Self alone. He, the Ātman, of whom no "unknowable thing" remains over, is sarvajña, omniscient. "Etad vai tat" — and what is that? That very thing which Naciketas asked, that which even the gods doubted, that which is other than dharma and adharma, that supreme Step of Viṣṇu beyond which there is nothing higher — that, verily, this is — that has now been ascertained, that is the meaning.
Ka_C02_S01_V04: By which Self one beholds both the dream-state and the waking-state, that great, all-pervading Ātman knowing, the wise man does not grieve.
Ka_C02_S01_V04::block-0:
Considering that, owing to its extreme subtlety, this very thing is hard to know, the śruti repeats again and again the same teaching. Svapnāntam — the middle of dream, that which is knowable in dream — this is the meaning. So too jāgaritāntam — the middle of waking, that which is knowable in the waking state. Both — svapna-jāgarita-antau — by which Ātman the world thus continually beholds — all this is to be supplied as before.

That mahāntam vibhum ātmānam — that great, all-pervading Self, mahāntam because greater than the great, vibhum because pervading all — having known it, having understood by direct apprehension in the form "I myself am that Paramātman," that dhīraḥ — the discriminating one — does not grieve. For when the Self is known as the very nature of the seer, there remains no occasion for grief, since all the supposed causes of grief, being non-Self, fall outside oneself.
Ka_C02_S01_V05: He who knows this honey-eater, the living Self, near at hand, the Lord of what is and what is to be — thereafter he does not seek to hide. This indeed is That.
Ka_C02_S01_V05::block-0:
Further: yaḥ kaścit — whosoever — imam — this — madhvadam — eater of honey, that is, enjoyer of the fruit of action — jīvam — the living self, the supporter of the assemblage of prāṇas and the rest — ātmānam — as the Self — veda — knows — antikāt — from near, that is, from close at hand — īśānam — the Ruler — bhūtabhavyasya — of the three times, past, present and future — tataḥ — thereafter, after that knowledge — ātmānam na vijugupsate — does not desire to conceal the Self, because he has attained fearlessness.

For only as long as one stands amid fear and considers the Ātman as anitya, non-eternal, does he wish to guard and hide the Self. But when he comes to know the Ātman as nitya and advaita — eternal and non-dual — then who would wish to hide what, and from what? "Etad vai tat" — as before.
Ka_C02_S01_V06: He who beholds Him who, born first from tapas, was born even before the waters, and who, having entered the cave, abides together with the elements — this indeed is That.
Ka_C02_S01_V06::block-0:
He who has been pointed out as the pratyagātman in the form of īśvara — the same is sarvātman, the All-Self. This the śruti now displays. Yaḥ kaścit — whatever mumukṣu — seeker of liberation — pūrvam — first, before all — tapasaḥ — from tapas, here meaning Brahman, of the nature of jñāna and the rest — jātam — born, that is, the arisen Hiraṇyagarbha. With reference to what is "pūrvam"? It is told: adbhyaḥ pūrvam — earlier than the waters — that is, earlier than the five elements together with the waters; the meaning is, not earlier than the waters alone but than the entire pañcabhūta-aggregate.

Ajāyata — was born, came into being. That Prathamaja — Hiraṇyagarbha, after producing the bodies of devas and the rest, having entered the heart-ākāśa — guhā — the cavity in the body of every living being — abides, perceiving sound and the rest, attended by the elements — bhūtebhiḥ — that is, by the kārya-karaṇa, the bodies and senses produced. Whoever beholds (vyapaśyat) Him so abiding — yaḥ paśyati — he, by such seeing, beholds none other than this very prakṛta Brahman — the very Brahman that has been throughout under discussion.
Ka_C02_S01_V07: She, the Aditi, made of all deities, who comes into being together with prāṇa, who, having entered the cave, abides — she who was born together with the elements — this indeed is That.
Ka_C02_S01_V07::block-0:
Further: yā — she who — sarvadevatāmayī — made up of all deities, of the very nature of all gods — prāṇena — in the form of Hiraṇyagarbha — sambhavati — comes into being from the Supreme Brahman — aditiḥ — "the eater," so called from the act of eating, that is, of consuming sound and the rest as objects of enjoyment — tām aditim, having entered the guhā as before, abiding therein.

The text further specifies her: yā — she who — bhūtebhiḥ — together with the elements, accompanied by them — vyajāyata — was born, came forth. The meaning is that this same all-pervading consciousness, taking up the role of "eater" of sense-objects through the prāṇas, and seated in the cavity of the heart of every embodied being together with the bhūtas, is none other than the very Brahman under discussion. "Etad vai tat" — and this same is That.
Ka_C02_S01_V08: Hidden between the two fire-sticks (araṇis), like a well-nourished embryo borne by pregnant women, is Jātavedas (the all-knowing fire); day after day Agni is to be worshipped by men who keep wakeful watch and bring oblations. This indeed is That.
Ka_C02_S01_V08::block-0:
Further, Jātavedas — the fire which, with reference to the sacrifice (adhiyajña), is hidden, established between the upper and lower araṇis (fire-drilling sticks), and which is the enjoyer of all oblations, and which, with reference to the Self (adhyātma), abides within the yogins — is, just as an embryo is well-nourished (subhṛta) in the world by pregnant women through wholesome food and the like, so too well-borne by ṛtviks and yogins. This is the meaning.

Further, day after day (dive dive) — every single day — He is praiseworthy (īḍya), to be hymned and saluted, in the sacrificial rite and in the heart, by performers of rites and by yogins who are wakeful (jāgṛvadbhiḥ), ever-vigilant and never heedless. By men (manuṣyebhiḥ) endowed with oblations (haviṣmadbhiḥ) — possessed of clarified butter and the like, and possessed of meditation and contemplative realisation — Agni is so worshipped. "This indeed is That" — that very Brahman which is the topic under discussion.
Ka_C02_S01_V09: From which the sun rises and into which it sets — in That are all the gods established, and none whatsoever transcends That. This indeed is That.
Ka_C02_S01_V09::block-0:
Further, that prāṇa from which the sun rises (udeti) — arises — and into which alone, day after day, it goes to setting (astam), to extinction and disappearance — into that prāṇa, that very Self, all the gods, namely Agni and the rest on the divine plane (adhidaivam), and Speech and the rest on the personal plane (adhyātmam), all of them, the entire universe, are fixed (arpitāḥ), entered into, just as spokes are fastened in the hub of a wheel, during the time of cosmic maintenance.

That prāṇa too is none other than Brahman. That, this all-pervading Brahman whose Self is everything — none whatsoever transcends It (na atyeti); none whosoever, by abandoning Its essential nature, attains otherness from It. "This indeed is That."
Ka_C02_S01_V10: What is here, that is there; what is there, that is here. From death to death he goes who sees here as if there were difference.
Ka_C02_S01_V10::block-0:
Lest anyone should suspect that what abides in beings, from Brahmā down to the immovable, being conditioned by those various adjuncts and so appearing as if non-Brahman, were transmigratory and other than the supreme Brahman, this is said. Whatever appears here, conjoined with the adjuncts of effect (body) and cause (organs) and seeming to the unwise to be characterised by the marks of saṃsāra — that very thing, abiding in its own Self, is yonder (amutra) Brahman: of the nature of eternal solid consciousness, free from all the marks of saṃsāra.

And what abides yonder, in that Self, that very thing — following along here, conditioned by the adjuncts of body, organs, name and form — is conceived; nothing else. Such being the case, deluded by avidyā which has the character of seeing differences arising from the natures of the adjuncts, whoever sees as it were difference (nāneva) here in Brahman, which is undifferentiated — thinking "I am other than the supreme; the supreme Brahman is other than me" — he, from death (mṛtyoḥ), from one dying, attains death (mṛtyum), the state of repeated birth and death, again and again. Therefore one should not so see. The purport of the sentence is: one should see, "I am verily Brahman, of the single savour of consciousness, unbroken, all-pervading like space, perfectly full."
Ka_C02_S01_V11: By the mind alone is this to be attained; there is here no diversity whatsoever. From death to death he goes who sees here as if there were difference.
Ka_C02_S01_V11::block-0:
Through the mind alone, prepared by the teacher and by the scriptures, prior to the realisation of unity, this Brahman of single savour — "It is the Self alone; there is nothing else" — is to be attained. And when It is attained, since avidyā which sets up the appearance of plurality has been removed, here in Brahman there is no diversity whatsoever (nānā nāsti kiñcana) — not even of the size of an atom.

But he who does not relinquish the vision born of the darkness of avidyā and sees here in Brahman as if there were diversity — he goes from death to death (mṛtyoḥ mṛtyum) indeed, by superimposing even the slightest difference. This is the meaning.
Ka_C02_S01_V12: The Puruṣa of the size of a thumb dwells in the middle of the body; knowing Him as the Lord of what has been and what is to be, one no longer seeks to hide oneself from Him. This indeed is That.
Ka_C02_S01_V12::block-0:
Once again He proclaims that very Brahman which is the topic — He is of the size of a thumb (aṅguṣṭha-mātraḥ), of thumb's measure. The lotus of the heart is of the size of a thumb; the inner organ which dwells in its cavity is the adjunct, and so He is called "thumb-measured," like the space within the joint of a bamboo of thumb's thickness.

Puruṣa: "by Him this whole universe is filled (pūrṇa)." He dwells in the middle, in the Self, that is, in the body. Knowing that Self as the Lord of what has been and what is to be (īśānaṃ bhūta-bhavyasya), "thereafter (na tataḥ) one does not shrink from Him" — and the rest is as before.
Ka_C02_S01_V13: The Puruṣa of the size of a thumb is like a smokeless flame, the Lord of what has been and what is to be. He alone is today, and He alone shall be tomorrow. This indeed is That.
Ka_C02_S01_V13::block-0:
Further, the Puruṣa of thumb's measure is like a smokeless flame (jyotir-iva adhūmakaḥ). "Smokeless" is appropriate because of His being supreme light. He who is thus contemplated by yogins in the heart, the Lord of what has been and what is to be — He alone, eternal, immutable, abiding now (adya) in living beings, He alone shall abide tomorrow (śvaḥ). No other equal to Him exists, and no other will arise. This is the meaning.

By this, the view that "some hold He does not exist" (Ka.U. 1.1.20) — though by reasoning it does not arise — is, by its own utterance through the Śruti, refuted; and so too is the doctrine of momentariness (kṣaṇabhaṅga-vāda).
Ka_C02_S01_V14: As water rained upon a height runs down upon the mountains, so he who sees the qualities (or selves) as separate runs after them indeed.
Ka_C02_S01_V14::block-0:
Once again, He sets forth the censure of seeing difference in Brahman. Just as water rained (vṛṣṭam) — sprinkled — on a difficult, lofty terrain runs (vidhāvati) down upon mountainous, low-lying regions, becoming scattered and so being lost; even so, he who sees the dharmas — which are non-different from the Self — as separate (pṛthak), seeing them as different in each body, runs after (anuvidhāvati) those very differences which conform to the bodies.

The meaning is: he attains the difference of body again and again, separately. He undergoes embodiment after embodiment, by reason of the difference in his vision.
Ka_C02_S01_V15: As pure water poured into pure water becomes verily one with it, so, O Gautama, becomes the Self of the muni who knows.
Ka_C02_S01_V15::block-0:
But for him who is endowed with knowledge, in whom the seeing of difference produced by adjuncts has been destroyed, who beholds the non-dual Self of single savour as utterly pure, solid consciousness — for the muni, the contemplative one, who thus knows — what is the nature of the Self? It is said: just as pure (śuddha), clear water poured (āsiktam) into pure, clear water becomes of one savour and not otherwise, even so does the Self become for the muni, the contemplative one who knows the unity, O Gautama.

Therefore, abandoning the seeing of difference taught by quarrelsome logicians and the false vision of the nāstikas, the vision of the unity of the Self, taught by the Veda which is more solicitous of one's welfare than a thousand mothers and fathers, is to be cherished by those whose pride is stilled. This is the meaning.
Ka_C02_S02_V01: The city of eleven gates belongs to the Unborn whose consciousness is undeflected. Having meditated upon Him, one does not grieve; and being released, one is liberated. This indeed is That.
Ka_C02_S02_V01::block-0:
Once again, by another mode, this fresh undertaking is for the firm ascertainment of the truth of Brahman, since Brahman is exceedingly difficult to know. Pura — "a city," so called because it is like a city; for, on observing the array of the city's appurtenances such as gates, gate-keepers, presiding officers, and the rest, the body is recognised as a pura. And a city, with its appurtenances, is everywhere seen to exist for the sake of a master who is himself uncompounded with it, independent, and sovereign. In the same way, by parity with cities in general, this body, though a compound of many appurtenances, must rightly exist for the sake of a master who, like the king on his throne, is uncompounded with it and unlike the city's own nature.

And this very pura called the body has eleven gates: seven in the head, three downward together with the navel, and one in the crown — by these eleven it is the city of eleven gates. Of whom is it the city? Of the Unborn (ajasya), of the Self who is free from birth and the rest of the modifications, who occupies the place of the king and whose nature is wholly distinct from the properties of the city. Avakra-cetasaḥ — whose consciousness, whose cognising power, is avakra, undeflected, uncrooked, ever abiding in one and the same form like the light of the sun: such is the One of straight consciousness. Of that Brahman, who stands as the king and to whom this city belongs, that supreme Lord and master of the pura, having performed (anuṣṭhāya) — that is, having meditated upon Him; for meditation, preceded by right knowledge, is the appropriate "performance" in His regard.

Having thus meditated upon Him as free from all hankerings, as the Same seated alike in all beings, one no longer grieves. For, fearlessness having been attained from the knowledge of Him, there remains no occasion for sorrow — whence then the apprehension of fear? Even here in this very life, he becomes released from the bonds of desires and works fashioned by avidyā. And being thus released, he is liberated — meaning, he no longer takes on a body again.
Ka_C02_S02_V02: He is the Swan dwelling in the pure region, the Vasu dwelling in the firmament, the Hotṛ dwelling at the altar, the Guest dwelling in the house; He dwells among men, dwells among the gods, dwells in the truth, dwells in space; born of waters, born of earth, born of sacrifice, born of mountains — the Truth, the Vast.
Ka_C02_S02_V02::block-0:
Yet that Self is not abiding in one city alone; rather, He dwells in every city. How so? Haṃsaḥ — so called because He goes (han, gam): He moves. Śuci-ṣat — He who, as the Self of the sun, sits in śuci, in the bright sky. Vasuḥ — He who causes all to dwell, the bestower of dwelling. Antarikṣa-sat — as the Self of vāyu, He sits in the firmament. Hotā — Agni, as the śruti declares, "Agni indeed is the Hotṛ." Vediṣat — He sits on the vedi, the earth, the place of the altar, as confirmed by the mantra, "This altar is the farthest end of the earth" (Ṛg-veda Maṇḍ. 1.22.164.35).

Atithi-duroṇa-sat — as Soma, the Guest, He sits in the duroṇa, the soma-pot; or, as the Brāhmaṇa-guest, He dwells in the duroṇas, the houses. Nṛ-ṣat — He sits among nṛs, among men. Vara-sat — He sits among the varas, the foremost ones, the gods. Ṛta-sat — ṛta is satya, truth, or the sacrifice; He sits in that. Vyoma-sat — He sits in vyoman, in space. Ab-jāḥ — born in the waters in the form of conch, oyster, alligator and the like. Go-jāḥ — born on the earth (go) in the form of paddy, barley, and so forth. Ṛta-jāḥ — born in the form of the limbs of sacrifice. Adri-jāḥ — born from the mountains in the form of rivers and the rest.

Though He thus is the Self of all, He remains ṛtam — of unfailing truth-nature itself. Bṛhat — vast, great, because He is the cause of all. And even when, by the same mantra, the sun alone is intended, the sun's identity with the very nature of the Self is itself acknowledged; therefore there is no contradiction in expounding the verse with reference to Brahman either. The purport of the mantra, then, is this: the Self of the universe is one alone, all-pervading; there is no plurality of selves.
Ka_C02_S02_V03: He drives the prāṇa upward, the apāna He hurls downward; in the middle, seated and worshipped, abides the Dwarf — Him all the gods adore.
Ka_C02_S02_V03::block-0:
An indication for the apprehension of the Self's true nature is now stated. Ūrdhvam — upward from the heart — He leads (unnayati) the prāṇa, the vital current called prāṇa, the vāyu in that operation. Likewise, the apāna, He pratyak — downward — asyati, casts; "He who does so" must be supplied as the remainder of the sentence.

Madhye — in the middle, in the space of the lotus of the heart — āsīnam, seated, manifest in the buddhi, the illuminator of cognition, vāmana — the worshipful, the worthy of being well honoured. Him, all the viśve devāḥ — the senses, the eye and the rest, the prāṇas — bringing as their tribute the cognitions of forms and the rest, upāsate, worship Him, just as subjects worship the king. The meaning is: keeping their activities ever directed toward Him, they do not desist. The purport of the sentence is: He for whose sake, and prompted by whom, all the activities of vāyu and the senses are set in motion — He, distinct from them, stands established.
Ka_C02_S02_V04: Of this embodied one, dwelling within the body, when it is breaking up, when it is being released from the body — what here remains? This indeed is That.
Ka_C02_S02_V04::block-0: Further, of this dehin, the embodied one, the Self dwelling in the body, when He is visraṃsamāna, falling away. The meaning of the term visraṃsana is then expressly stated by the words "deha-vimucyamānasya" — being released from the body. Kim atra pariśiṣyate — what remains here, in the aggregate of prāṇa and the rest? Nothing whatever remains. Just as, on the king's flight, the dwellers of the city scatter, in like manner, here in this body, the Self being He on whose departure, in but a moment, this whole assemblage of effect (the body) and instrument (the senses) becomes shorn of strength, shattered, utterly destroyed — that Self, distinct from them all, stands established.
Ka_C02_S02_V05: Not by prāṇa, not by apāna, does any mortal live; but they live by another, on whom these two depend.
Ka_C02_S02_V05::block-0:
It might be supposed (pūrvapakṣa): it is by the very departure of prāṇa, apāna and the rest that this aggregate becomes shattered, and not by the departure of any Self that is distinct from them; the mortal lives here by means of prāṇa and the rest themselves. — This (siddhānta) is not so: na prāṇena, na apānena — neither by prāṇa nor by apāna nor by eye and the rest does any mortal — any embodied man — kaścana, anyone whatsoever, jīvati, live. For these are para-artha — exist for another's sake; being agents that act only by combining together, their being a cause of life is not logically established.

It is nowhere seen in the world that things which are themselves combinations exist of themselves, without being employed by another, distinct, uncombined being who is their own master — as houses and the like in worldly experience. So too with prāṇa and the rest: being themselves of a combined nature, they too must exist for another. Hence, itareṇa tu — but by the other alone, by Him who is wholly different from the combined prāṇa and the like, do all these combined things jīvanti, live, sustain their breaths.

Yasmin — in whom, the Self distinct from all that is compounded, the Supreme — etau, these two, prāṇa and apāna, together with the eye and other senses, all combined, upāśritau, abide as dependent. He for whose sake, the uncompounded One, prāṇa, apāna and the rest, themselves compounded, perform every operation — He, distinct from them, stands established. This is the import.
Ka_C02_S02_V06: Come now, I shall declare to thee this hidden, eternal Brahman, and how, having met with death, the Self fares, O Gautama.
Ka_C02_S02_V06::block-0: Hanta — "come now," at this moment, once again to thee — te, tubhyam — idam, this guhyam, secret, to be guarded, sanātanam, eternal, ancient, brahma, I shall declare (pravakṣyāmi). That, by knowing which, the entire round of saṃsāra ceases, and by not knowing which, transmigration occurs — and how, on meeting with death, the Self comes to be, that is, how the Self transmigrates — that, O Gautama, hear thou.
Ka_C02_S02_V07: Some embodied beings enter into a womb for the obtaining of a body; others go on to the stationary — each according to his works, each according to his learning.
Ka_C02_S02_V07::block-0:
Yonim — into the womb-gate — endowed with the seed of semen, anye, certain other persons, ignorant and deluded, prapadyante, enter, śarīratvāya — for the sake of obtaining a body — being dehinaḥ, embodied: that is, they enter the womb. Sthāṇum — the stationary state of trees and the like — anye, others, the most degraded, on attaining death, anusaṃyanti — go after, follow.

Yathā-karma — "as is each one's karma, so accordingly": the meaning is — under the sway of whatever sort of karma each has performed in this birth. And tathā yathā-śrutam — and likewise, in conformity with whatever knowledge has been acquired, they obtain a body precisely answering to it. As another śruti declares: "The births are in accordance with one's prajñā" (Aitareya Āraṇyaka 2.3.2).
Ka_C02_S02_V08: He who, while these are asleep, keeps watch — that Person, fashioning desire after desire — He alone is the Pure, He is Brahman, He alone is called the Immortal. On Him all the worlds rest, and none whatsoever transcends Him. This indeed is That.
Ka_C02_S02_V08::block-0:
What was promised — "the secret Brahman I shall declare" — that He now declares: He who, supteṣu, when prāṇa and the rest are asleep, jāgarti, keeps watch and does not slumber. How? Kāmaṃ kāmam — desire after desire, that and that intended object, woman and the rest, nirmimāṇaḥ, fashioning, bringing forth by avidyā: who, as the Puruṣa, thus keeps watch — He alone is the śukram, the bright, the pure; He alone is that Brahman; there is no other secret Brahman besides this. He alone is amṛtam, the imperishable, so called in all the śāstras.

Further, the worlds — earth and the rest — all of them — śritāḥ, take refuge, depend, in Him alone, in Brahman, since He is the cause of all the worlds. "Tad u nātyeti kaścana" — "and none whatsoever transcends Him" — and the rest is to be construed exactly as before.
Ka_C02_S02_V09: Just as fire, though one, having entered the world, becomes corresponding in form to every form, even so the one inner Self of all beings becomes corresponding to every form, and yet remains outside.
Ka_C02_S02_V09::block-0:
Therefore, in the inward organs of those whose minds have been unsettled by the intellects of bad logicians and heretics (kutārkika-pāṣaṇḍa), the knowledge of the unity of the Self — though established by the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) and proclaimed again and again — does not take hold in the hearts of brāhmaṇas of un-straight intellect (anṛju-buddhi). Hence, intent upon making it firmly grasped, the śruti, with great care, repeats it once more: "agniḥ yathā" — just as fire, being in essence one and of the very nature of light, having entered bhuvanam — "that in which the bhūtas come to be is bhuvana," namely this world — that is, having pervaded it, becomes prati-rūpa to every rūpa rūpam, that is, in conformity with the variety of the combustibles such as wood and the like; thus it became multiform there and there, by the difference of the fuels.

In just the same way, the one inner Self of all beings, being most subtle, has, as it were, entered into every body — as fire enters into wood and similar fuels — and so has become "prati-rūpa," corresponding to every form (rūpaṃ rūpam) within all beings; and yet, outside (bahiḥ ca), it abides in its own unmodified form, even like ākāśa.
Ka_C02_S02_V10: Just as air, though one, having entered the world, becomes corresponding in form to every form, even so the one inner Self of all beings becomes corresponding to every form, and yet remains outside.
Ka_C02_S02_V10::block-0: Likewise, another illustration: "vāyur yathaikaḥ" and so on. Air has, in the form of prāṇa, entered into bodies. "It became corresponding to every form" — and the rest is identical with the previous mantra.
Ka_C02_S02_V11: Just as the sun, the eye of the whole world, is not soiled by the external blemishes seen by the eye, even so the one inner Self of all beings is not soiled by the suffering of the world, being outside it.
Ka_C02_S02_V11::block-0:
Now an objection presents itself (pūrvapakṣa): if the one Self is the Self of all, then the misery of saṃsāra would attach to the Supreme alone. To this the siddhānta is now stated: "sūryo yathā" — just as the sun, by its illumination, helps the eye and thereby reveals impure things such as urine and ordure, becoming thus the eye, as it were, of the entire world that beholds them, yet, being one, is not soiled either by the inward (ādhyātmika) sins consequent upon seeing such impurities, or by the outward defects of contact with those impurities — even so the inner Self of all beings, being outside (bāhyaḥ), is not soiled by the suffering of the world.

For the world, by virtue of avidyā which is superimposed (adhyastā) on the Self, undergoes suffering arising from desire and action; but in truth this does not really attach to its own Self. Just as on a rope, on a mother-of-pearl, on the inside of an oyster-shell, and on the sky, the imagined snake, silver, water, and dirt are not by their own nature defects intrinsic to the rope and the rest — but only when there is contact with these, owing to the superimposition of contrary cognition (viparīta-buddhi-adhyāsa), are they conceived as if possessed of those defects; nor are the rope and the rest tainted by those defects, for they stand outside that very superimposition of contrary cognition — even so, in the Self, the entire world superimposes the wrong notion, of the form of action, agent and fruit (kriyā-kāraka-phala), corresponding to the snake and so forth, and on account of that superimposition undergoes the misery of birth, death and the like; but the Self, although it is the Self of the whole world, is not soiled by the suffering of the world brought about by that contrary superimposition.

Why not? "bāhyaḥ" — for, just like the rope and so on, He stands outside (bāhya) the superimposition of contrary cognition.
Ka_C02_S02_V12: The one Controller, the inner Self of all beings, who makes his one form manifold — the wise who behold Him as seated within their own self attain eternal bliss; not the others.
Ka_C02_S02_V12::block-0:
Further: He, indeed, is the Supreme Lord (parameśvara) — all-pervading, independent, one (eka); there is none equal to Him nor any other surpassing Him. He is vaśī, the Controller, for this entire world stands under His sway. Why? Because He is the inner Self of all beings (sarva-bhūta-antar-ātmā). It is He who, being one, of one taste alone, of the nature of pure consciousness condensed (viśuddha-vijñāna-ghana-rūpa), through the difference of impure adjuncts (upādhi) such as name and form, makes the one form manifold (bahudhā), of many kinds — and that merely by His own being, owing to His inconceivable power (acintya-śakti).

That very Self, abiding within (ātma-stham), means: manifested in the form of consciousness in the buddhi within the heart-space (hṛdayākāśa) of one's own body — for the body is not the support of the Self, since the Self, like ākāśa, is formless (amūrta); the analogy is rather that of the face seen in a mirror (ādarśastham mukham). Him, this Lord-Self, those who, having turned their inclinations away from external objects (nivṛtta-bāhya-vṛtti), behold (anupaśyanti) — that is, directly experience following the instruction of the teacher and the scripture (ācāryāgamopadeśam anu) — those wise discriminators (dhīrāḥ vivekinaḥ), who have themselves become the Supreme Lord, attain eternal, unceasing bliss whose mark is the bliss of the Self (ātmānanda-lakṣaṇa); not the others, those of un-discerning intellect addicted to externals — not even though it is their own Self — because of the obstruction of avidyā (avidyā-vyavadhānāt).
Ka_C02_S02_V13: The Eternal among the eternals, the Conscious among the conscious — the One who, though one, dispenses the desires of the many — the wise who behold Him as seated within their own self attain eternal peace; not the others.
Ka_C02_S02_V13::block-0:
Further: "nityaḥ" — imperishable; "of the imperishable" — that is, of the imperishable ones. "cetanaḥ" — the conscious; "of the conscious" — that is, of the conscious living beings such as Brahmā and the rest. Just as the burning property of non-fires such as water and so on is on account of fire, even so the consciousness of others is on account of the consciousness of the Self alone (ātma-caitanya-nimitta).

Further, He, the Omniscient Lord of all (sarva-jña, sarveśvara), is the One who, all alone, effortlessly dispenses (vidadhāti, prayacchati) to the many desirers in saṃsāra their desired objects — that is, the fruits of action conformably to their action (karma-anurūpam), and likewise the desired things granted out of His own grace (sva-anugraha-nimitta).

That very One abiding within the self (ātma-stham), the wise (dhīrāḥ) behold; for them, peace (śāntiḥ) — that is, complete cessation (uparati) — is eternal, ever-abiding, of the very nature of their own Self. Not for others, those who are not of this kind.
Ka_C02_S02_V14: "This is That" — thus they apprehend the indescribable, supreme bliss. How may I know That? Does It shine forth, or does It manifestly shine?
Ka_C02_S02_V14::block-0:
That bliss of the knowledge of the Self which is anirdeśya — incapable of being pointed out — supreme (paramam), most exalted (prakṛṣṭam), beyond the reach of the speech and mind of the ordinary man (prākṛta-puruṣa-vāṅ-manasayoḥ agocaram) — though it is so, those brāhmaṇas in whom the longings (eṣaṇā) have ceased apprehend it as "this very thing, immediately present" (tad etat pratyakṣam eva).

"How indeed (kathaṁ nu) — by what means — may I make known to myself that bliss?" — that is, may I bring it within the sphere of cognition under the form "this is It" (idam iti), as do those self-controlled ones (yati) whose longing for sense-objects has ceased.

"Does It shine (bhāti) — does It blaze, since It is of the nature of light? — and does It thereby become manifest (vibhāti) — clearly perceived as an object of our buddhi — or not?"
Ka_C02_S02_V15: There the sun does not shine, nor the moon and stars, nor do these lightnings shine — how then this fire? Him alone shining, all shine after Him; by His light all this shines forth.
Ka_C02_S02_V15::block-0:
Here is the answer: indeed, It does shine and It does illumine. How? "na tatra" — there, in that Brahman which is the very Self, even the sun, illuminator of all, does not shine; the sense is, it does not illumine that Brahman. Likewise, neither the moon and stars (na candratārakam), nor these lightnings (nemā vidyutaḥ); how then this fire (kuto'yam agniḥ) which is within the range of our perception?

What more need be said? — whatever shines, sun and the rest, all of it shines after Him alone — that is, after the Supreme Lord who is shining (bhāntam), blazing — "anubhāti," follows Him in shining. As a torch in water, or a firebrand, joined to fire, burns only after the burning fire and not of itself, even so. By His light alone (tasya bhāsā), by His radiance, all this — sun and so forth — shines forth (vibhāti).

Since this is so, that Brahman alone shines and shines forth manifestly. By the diverse light located in His effects, the very nature of Brahman as light-formed (bhā-rūpatva) is understood by itself (svataḥ); for that which has no shining of its own cannot bring about the shining of another — for jars and the like are not seen to illumine others, while sun and the like, which are of the nature of light, are so seen.
Ka_C02_S03_V01: With its root above and its branches below, this aśvattha is sanātana. That alone is pure, That is Brahman, That alone is called the immortal. On That all the worlds rest; none whatever transcends That. This indeed is That.
Ka_C02_S03_V01::block-0:
Just as in the world the apprehension of a tree's root is effected through the apprehension of its tuft (tūla), so by the apprehension of the saṃsāra-tree which is the effect, the desire is to ascertain the very nature (svarūpa) of its root, Brahman. With this aim, the present sixth valli is begun.

"ūrdhva-mūlaḥ" — having its root above; that is, that whose root is the supreme abode of Viṣṇu (tad viṣṇoḥ paramaṁ padam) — this very saṃsāra-tree, beginning with the unmanifest (avyakta) and ending with the immobile (sthāvara), is "having its root above." And it is called vṛkṣa (tree) because of vraścana — being liable to be hewn down — owing to its perishable nature (vinaśvaratva).

Its nature is that of the manifold misfortunes — birth, old age, death, sorrow and the rest, unbroken; its essence is otherwise from moment to moment (pratikṣaṇam anyathā-svabhāvaḥ); like the city of the gandharvas, like a mirage of water (māyā-marīcy-udaka-gandharva-nagara), its very form is seen only to be lost; and at the end, like a tree, it is reduced to non-being (abhāvātmaka); like the trunk of a plantain, void of pith (niḥsāra); the field on which the conjectures of hundreds of heretical intellects (pāṣaṇḍa-buddhi-vikalpa) play; whose true "thisness" (idantattva) is not ascertained by those eager to know reality; whose root-essence (mūla-sāra) is the supreme Brahman established by Vedānta.

Its seed-source is avidyā, desire, action, and the unmanifest (avidyā-kāma-karma-avyakta-bīja); its sprout is hiraṇyagarbha — composed of the two powers of jñāna and kriyā belonging to the lower Brahman (apara-brahma); its trunks are the various species of living beings; its swelling pride springs from the watering of the cravings appropriate to each; its tender shoots are the buddhi, the senses and the objects (buddhi-indriya-viṣaya-pravālāṅkura); its leaves are the teachings of the śruti, smṛti, nyāya, and vidyās; its fair blossoms are the many actions — sacrifice, gift, austerity and the rest; its many tastes are the experiences of pleasure and pain; its endless fruits are what the creatures live upon; with the constant sprinkling of the water of those very cravings its roots have grown matted and firmly bound; in it the birds — beings up to Brahmā, in the seven worlds beginning with satya — have made their nests; the great roar arising in it is the tumult made by all the manifold sounds — dance, song, instruments, hooting, slapping, laughter, shouting, weeping, "alas!" "let go! let go!" and so on, born of the joys and griefs arising in living beings; its felling is brought about by the sword of non-attachment (asaṅga-śastra), forged from the realization of the Self as Brahman (brahmātma-darśana) which is enjoined in the Vedānta.

This saṃsāra-tree is "aśvattha" — like the aśvattha-fig, eternally tossed about, whose nature is to be never the same, by the winds of desire and action (kāma-karma-vāta-īrita). With its branches of heaven, hell, beasts, ghosts and so on it is "avāk-śākhaḥ" — having its branches downward (avāñco yasya śākhāḥ). It is "sanātana," of long-standing duration, since it has no beginning (anāditvāt cira-pravṛttaḥ).

Whatever is the root of this saṃsāra-tree, that very thing is "śukra" — bright, pure, luminous, of the very nature of the light of consciousness as the Self (caitanyātma-jyotiḥ-svabhāva). That alone is Brahman, since it is greater than all (sarva-mahattvāt). That alone is called "amṛta," since its very nature is imperishable (avināśa-svabhāva), being said so because of its truth (satyatvāt). "All modification (vikāra) is rooted in speech and is mere name; the unreal is other than this, mortal" (vācārambhaṇaṁ vikāro nāmadheyam, anṛtam, anyad ato martyam — Chānd. 6.1.4 etc.).

In that supremely real Brahman, all the worlds rest, in their origination, continuance, and dissolution — worlds that are like the city of the gandharvas, the water of a mirage, like māyā, the appearance of which is recognized to lack the perception of the supreme reality. "tad u nātyeti kaścana" — none whatever, no modification, transcends that Brahman, even as the effects pot and the like do not transcend their material clay (mṛd-ādi). This indeed is That.
Ka_C02_S03_V02: Whatever this whole world is, having issued forth, vibrates in Prāṇa (the supreme Brahman). It is the great fear, the upraised thunderbolt; those who know This become immortal.
Ka_C02_S03_V02::block-0:
It might be objected: that very Brahman, said to be the root of the world and by knowing which one becomes immortal, does not exist; this world has issued forth from non-being alone. To refute this it is said — whatever this entire world is, vibrates, that is, trembles, while abiding in Prāṇa, the supreme Brahman; having issued and gone forth from That alone, it moves and acts under fixed regulation.

That Brahman, which is thus the cause of the world's origin and so on, is the great fear: it is great and it is fear, since on its account every being is afraid — hence "great fear"; it is like an upraised thunderbolt. Just as servants, seeing their master facing them with thunderbolt-raised hand, conduct themselves under strict regulation according to his command, even so this world — characterised by the moon, sun, planets, constellations and stars — together with its presiding lords moves under fixed regulation, without rest even for a moment. This is the meaning conveyed.

Those who know This — the one Brahman that is the witness of the activity of one's own Self — become immortal, possessed of the nature of deathlessness.
Ka_C02_S03_V03: Through fear of Him fire burns; through fear the sun shines; through fear Indra and Vāyu, and Death the fifth, hasten on their courses.
Ka_C02_S03_V03::block-0: How does the world function out of fear of Him? This is answered — through fear, that is, through dread of this supreme Lord, fire burns; through fear the sun shines; through fear Indra and Vāyu, and Death the fifth, run on. For unless these world-rulers, who are themselves mighty lords, had a controller standing as it were with thunderbolt upraised, the regulated activity proper to servants frightened by their master's fear would not be intelligible in their case.
Ka_C02_S03_V04: If one has been able to realise Him here, before the falling of the body, then in the various creations and worlds one becomes fit for embodiment (i.e. is born again). (If one fails, one continues in saṃsāra.)
Ka_C02_S03_V04::block-0:
If here, that is, while still living, one has been able — being competent, has come to know — to realise Brahman, the cause of fear, before the falling away, the dropping, of the body, then one is freed from the bondage of saṃsāra. But if one has not been able to realise It, then, owing to that non-realisation, in the creations — those in which beings to be created are projected, viz. the worlds beginning with earth — and in those worlds one becomes fit for embodiment, that is, capable of taking on a body; the meaning is that one assumes a body.

Therefore, before the falling of the body, effort must be made for the realisation of the Self, since here itself the seeing of the Self, like that of one's face in a mirror, can take place clearly, but not in other worlds — except in Brahmaloka. And that (Brahmaloka realisation) is exceedingly hard to obtain.
Ka_C02_S03_V05: As in a mirror, so in oneself; as in a dream, so in the world of the fathers; as seen in water, so in the world of the gandharvas; and as light and shade, so in Brahmaloka.
Ka_C02_S03_V05::block-0:
How is it so? It is explained — just as in a mirror people see their own image as a reflection, perfectly distinct, so here, in the Self — that is, in one's own intellect, when it has become spotless like a mirror — there occurs a distinct seeing of the Self. This is the meaning.

Just as in a dream the seeing is indistinct, springing up from the impressions of the waking state, so in the world of the fathers the seeing of the Self is likewise indistinct, owing to attachment to the enjoyment of the fruits of action. And just as in water one sees one's form as it were reflected with its parts indistinct, so in the world of the gandharvas the seeing of the Self is indistinct. So too is it understood, on the authority of scripture, with regard to other worlds.

Like light and shade — that is, exceedingly distinct — is the seeing only in the one Brahmaloka. And that is hard to attain, since it is achievable only by exceptionally distinguished works and knowledge. Therefore, for the seeing of the Self, effort must be made here itself — this is the purport.
Ka_C02_S03_V06: Knowing the separateness of the senses (from the Self) and their rising and setting, since they originate apart, the wise one does not grieve.
Ka_C02_S03_V06::block-0:
How is He to be realised? And what is the purpose of realising Him? It is answered — of the senses, namely the ear and the rest, which originate separately from their own causes such as ākāśa and so on for the purpose of grasping their respective objects, one must know their separateness from the absolutely pure, kevala, mere-consciousness Self-nature, that is, their being of a nature wholly different from the Self's own nature.

Likewise, of those very senses, the rising and setting — that is, the origination and dissolution apparent through the cognition of the waking and dream states — belong to them and not to the Self. Knowing this through discrimination, the wise one — the man of intellect — does not grieve, because, owing to the Self's nature being eternal and one and undeviating, the cause of sorrow cannot apply to It.

Thus too another scripture states: "The knower of the Self crosses sorrow" (Chā. Up. 7.1.3).
Ka_C02_S03_V07: Higher than the senses is the mind; higher than the mind is the intellect (sattva); higher than the intellect is the great Self (mahān ātmā); higher than that great is the Unmanifest (avyakta).
Ka_C02_S03_V07::block-0:
Since the separateness of the senses from the Self has been spoken of, He is not to be sought outside; for that very Self, being the inner Self, is the Self of all. How then is He to be realised? It is answered — "higher than the senses is the mind", and so on. Here, since objects belong to the same class as the senses, by mentioning the senses the objects too are included.

The rest is as before. By the word sattva the intellect (buddhi) is meant here.
Ka_C02_S03_V08: Higher than the Unmanifest is Puruṣa, all-pervading and devoid of any mark (liṅga). Knowing whom, the creature is liberated and attains immortality.
Ka_C02_S03_V08::block-0:
But higher than the Unmanifest is Puruṣa, all-pervading, since He is the cause even of all the pervading things such as ākāśa and the rest. He is alinga: that by which something is inferred or known is its mark — viz. the intellect and the rest; He in whom there is no such mark is alinga, that is, devoid of all the qualities of saṃsāra.

Knowing whom — through a teacher and through scripture — the creature is liberated, while still living, from the heart-knots of avidyā and so on; and even when the body falls he attains immortality.

He is alinga, higher than the Unmanifest, Puruṣa — this connects with the previous (verse).
Ka_C02_S03_V09: His form does not stand within the range of vision; no one sees Him with the eye. He is grasped through the heart, by deliberation, by the mind; those who know This become immortal.
Ka_C02_S03_V09::block-0:
How then can the seeing of that markless One be intelligible? It is answered — His form, that of the inner Self, does not stand within the range of vision, the field of being seen. Hence no one — that is, none whatsoever — sees, that is, apprehends, by the eye, by any sense (the mention of the eye standing for all senses), this Self that is the topic.

How then is He to be seen? It is answered — through the heart, that is, the intellect that abides in the heart; manīṣā: the mind, having the form of saṃkalpa and the rest, is governed by the īṣ (the controller) — hence manīṭ; manīṣā is by that, the intellect free from doubt and alternatives. By the mind, in the form of meditation, that is, by right realisation, He is abhiklṛpta — perfectly accomplished, fully revealed. The implied completion is: "the Self can be known".

Those who know That Self, this Brahman, become immortal.
Ka_C02_S03_V10: When the five organs of knowledge stand still together with the manas, and when the buddhi too no longer stirs — that, they declare, is the highest state.
Ka_C02_S03_V10::block-0:
How is that supreme state, attainable only in the cave of the heart, to be reached? With this purpose in view, yoga is now expounded.

'Yadā' — at that time when the five jñānas, withdrawn from their respective objects, abide solely in the Ātman. Because they are the means of knowledge (jñāna-arthatvāt), the senses beginning with the ear are themselves termed 'jñānāni' here. They 'avatiṣṭhante' — stand firm — 'saha manasā' — together with the manas, that is, accompanied by the manas, by that inner organ (antaḥkaraṇa) which has itself turned away from saṅkalpa and the rest of its activity.

'Buddhiśca' — and the buddhi, whose defining mark is determination (adhyavasāya-lakṣaṇā), 'na viceṣṭati' — does not stir, does not engage in its own operations, is not employed. That state, the seers call the highest goal — paramā gati.
Ka_C02_S03_V11: That state — the steady holding of the senses — they regard as yoga. Then one becomes vigilant, undistracted; for yoga has both arising and passing away.
Ka_C02_S03_V11::block-0:
'Tām' — that very state of such a kind — 'yogam iti manyante': they regard as yoga, though it is in truth a viyoga, a disjunction. For this state of the yogin is precisely the disjunction from union with all that is anartha (every misery-yielding bond). In this state alone, the Ātman, freed from every adhyāropa of avidyā, abides established in its own true nature (svarūpa-pratiṣṭha).

'Sthirām indriya-dhāraṇām' — a steady, unshaken holding of the senses, that is, the firm restraint of the outer and inner organs alike. 'Apramattaḥ' — free from heedlessness, ever exerting himself toward samādhāna — 'tadā' — at that time, that is, when yoga has arisen — this is understood by the force of the words. For where there is no operation of the buddhi and the rest, there can be no occasion for pramāda.

Therefore, even prior to the cessation of buddhi's activity, apramāda is enjoined. Or alternatively: at the very moment when the holding of the senses has become steady, then itself, unimpeded apramattatva (vigilance) prevails — this is what is meant by 'apramattas tadā bhavati'.

Why so? 'Yogo hi prabhava-apyayau' — because yoga is of the nature of arising and passing away (upajana-apāya-dharmaka). Hence, in order to ward off its passing away, apramāda must be practised — this is the import.
Ka_C02_S03_V12: Not by speech, not by manas, not by the eye is It attainable. How can It be apprehended otherwise than by him who declares 'It is'?
Ka_C02_S03_V12::block-0:
Pūrvapakṣa: If Brahman were the object of the operations of buddhi etc., it could be grasped distinctly as 'this is It'. But on the cessation of buddhi etc., the means of apprehension being absent, Brahman remains unapprehended — and what is unapprehended simply 'is not'. For in the world it is established that what falls within the range of the instruments of cognition exists, and the contrary is non-existent (asat). Hence yoga is futile, and Brahman, being unapprehended, must be taken as non-existent. To this nāstika-objection, the reply now follows.

Siddhānta: Granted — true it is that Brahman cannot be attained by speech, nor by manas, nor by the eye, nor by any other sense; this much is conceded. Yet, even though devoid of every distinguishing mark, It is, since It is known to be the root (mūla) of the world; for the dissolution of effects (kārya-pravilāpana) terminates in being (astitva-niṣṭhatvāt). For this very effect — the world — when traced through gradations of subtlety in unbroken succession, leads the buddhi to rest precisely upon Sat. And when the buddhi itself, dissolving objects one after another, comes to be dissolved, even then it dissolves only as one whose womb is the cognition 'It is' (sat-pratyaya-garbha).

The buddhi indeed is our pramāṇa for ascertaining the true nature of the existent and the non-existent. If the world had no root, this effect would be wholly bound up with non-being and would be apprehended simply as 'asat, asat'. But that is not so; it is apprehended only as 'sat, sat' — just as the effects clay-pot etc. are apprehended as imbued with their cause clay etc. Hence the Ātman, the root of the world, is to be apprehended as 'It is' alone.

Why? 'Astīti bruvataḥ' — for him who declares 'It is', who follows the import of the āgama, who has śraddhā — and not 'anyatra', that is, in the nāstika who, of perverse vision, holds that the world has no Self as its root, that this effect is without continuity (niranvaya) and dissolves into utter non-being — how can that Brahman be apprehended in its true nature? In no way whatever — that is the meaning.
Ka_C02_S03_V13: It is to be apprehended only as 'It is', and through Its true essential nature, in respect of both. When apprehended thus as 'It is', Its essential nature reveals itself.
Ka_C02_S03_V13::block-0:
Therefore, casting aside the āsura position of the asad-vādin, the Ātman is to be apprehended as 'It is' alone — first through the upādhis of sat-kārya, the buddhi and the rest. But when the Ātman is grasped as devoid of these, as immutable (avikriya), and the effect is seen to have no being apart from the cause — as declared by the śruti, 'vācārambhaṇaṁ vikāro nāmadheyaṁ mṛttiketyeva satyam' (Chā. Up. 6.1.4) — then the tattva-bhāva of that Ātman, niḥ-upādhika, alinga, freed from being the object of the cognitions sat, asat and the rest, becomes manifest. And it is in this aspect that the Ātman is to be apprehended — that is the continuing import.

There too, of the two — the existence-aspect (astitva) characterised by upādhi and the essential-nature aspect (tattva-bhāva) free of upādhi — the genitive 'ubhayoḥ' is one of selection (nirdhāraṇa). Of him who has first apprehended the Ātman as 'It is' — that is, who has grasped It through the cognition of existence conditioned by the upādhi of sat-kārya — afterwards, when every form of upādhi has set, the tattva-bhāva of the Ātman, distinct from both the known and the unknown, of the nature of non-duality, indicated by the śruti as 'neti neti', 'asthūlam, anaṇu, ahrasvam', 'adṛśye 'nātmye 'nirukte 'nilayane' and so forth — that essential nature 'prasīdati', becomes graciously revealed, turns face-to-face. The clause 'one who has first apprehended It as It is' is what enables the Ātman's self-revelation.
Ka_C02_S03_V14: When all the desires that lodge in his heart are wholly loosed, then the mortal becomes immortal; here itself he attains Brahman.
Ka_C02_S03_V14::block-0:
Thus, for him who has come to see the Self in its paramārthic truth, when — at that time — all 'kāmas' (desires), since there is now nothing further to be desired apart from the Self, 'pramucyante' — are loosened, fall asunder; those kāmas which, prior to the dawn of true knowledge in this knower, were 'hṛdi śritāḥ' — lodged in the buddhi. For desires lodge in the buddhi, not in the Ātman, as is also taught by another śruti, 'kāmaḥ saṅkalpaḥ' (Bṛ. Up. 1.5.3) and the rest.

'Atha' — then; he who, prior to true knowledge, was a mortal, after that awakening becomes immortal through the destruction of mṛtyu whose marks are avidyā, kāma and karma; for, with the destruction of the very mṛtyu that prompts movement, no further going is possible.

'Atra' — here itself, in this very life, like the extinguishing of a lamp, with the cessation of every bond he 'brahma samaśnute' — he attains Brahman, that is to say, he becomes Brahman alone — that is the meaning.
Ka_C02_S03_V15: When all the knots of the heart are here cut asunder, then the mortal becomes immortal — this much, indeed, is the entire teaching.
Ka_C02_S03_V15::block-0:
But when, then, does the radical destruction of desires occur? It is now told. 'Yadā' — when 'sarve' all 'prabhidyante' — break apart, perish — 'hṛdayasya' of the buddhi, 'iha' here itself, while one is yet alive, the 'granthayaḥ' — knots, that is, the avidyā-cognitions which bind firmly like a knot.

Such are: 'I am this body', 'this wealth is mine', 'I am happy, I am sorrowing', and so on. Through the rise of the contrary cognition — the cognition of the Self as Brahman — 'I am Brahman alone, free of saṁsāra' — when the avidyā-knots are destroyed, the desires which depend upon them perish at the very root.

'Atha martyo'mṛto bhavati' — then the mortal becomes immortal. 'Etāvad-dhi' — this much alone, just this much, no more — let no doubt arise (that anything further is required). 'Anuśāsanam' — the teaching, the upadeśa — of all the Vedāntas — this is to be supplied to complete the sentence.
Ka_C02_S03_V16: A hundred and one are the nāḍīs of the heart; of these, one issues forth piercing the crown. Going upward through that, one reaches immortality; the others serve, at exit, for departure in various directions.
Ka_C02_S03_V16::block-0:
For the knower who, by the recognition of the Brahman-Self that is all-pervading and devoid of every distinction (niraśta-aśeṣa-viśeṣa-vyāpi), has had the entire knot of avidyā etc. cleft asunder, who has even while living become Brahman, there is no 'gati' — no going — at all; for it has been said 'atra brahma samaśnute' (Ka. Up. 2.3.14), and another śruti also declares, 'na tasya prāṇā utkrāmanti, brahmaiva san brahmāpyeti' (Bṛ. Up. 4.4.6).

But for those who are mandra-brahma-vits (knowers of the lower Brahman) and for those who have practised other vidyās and are entitled to brahma-loka, and again for those of contrary kind who only attain saṁsāra — for these is now described this special gati, by way of praising the fruit of the upapanna-superior brahma-vidyā here in question. Moreover, the agni-vidyā has earlier been asked about and answered; the manner of attaining its fruit must also be told. With these objects the mantras commence.

'Śatam ca' — a hundred — 'ekā ca' — and one, named Suṣumnā — are the nāḍīs (sirās) of a man, issuing from the heart. Among them, piercing the crown and going forth, is that single one named Suṣumnā. By that nāḍī, at the time of death, having yoked the Self in the heart, he should join. Going upward through that nāḍī through the door of the sun, one reaches āpekṣika-amṛtatva — relative immortality, in the sense of being-state until the dissolution of all beings — as the smṛti declares, 'ābhūta-samplavaṁ sthānam amṛtatvaṁ hi bhāṣyate' (Vi. Pu. 2.8.97); or, after enjoying unequalled enjoyments in brahma-loka, in due course attains, together with Brahmā, the principal mukhya-amṛtatva.

'Viṣvaṅ' — variously, in many directions — the other nāḍīs serve at the time of utkramaṇa (exit) merely as the cause of saṁsāra — that is, they serve only for the further attainment of saṁsāra, that is the meaning.
Ka_C02_S03_V17: Of the size of a thumb is the Puruṣa, the Inner Self, ever seated in the heart of beings; one should draw Him out from one's body as one draws a stalk from the muñja-grass, with steadfastness. One should know Him as pure, immortal — yea, one should know Him as pure, immortal.
Ka_C02_S03_V17::block-0:
Now, for the purpose of summing up the import of all the vallīs, He says — 'aṅguṣṭha-mātraḥ puruṣaḥ' — the Puruṣa, of the measure of a thumb, the antarātman, is ever seated in the heart of all beings, in the manner already expounded. 'Tam' — Him — 'svāt śarīrāt' — from one's own body — 'pravṛhet' — one should draw out, raise out, extract, separate — that is the meaning.

Like what? It is told — 'muñjād iva iṣīkām' — as one draws out the iṣīkā-stalk that lies within the muñja-grass — 'dhairyeṇa' — by steadfastness, by apramāda. Him, drawn out from the body — pure cit-mātra — one should know — 'vidyāt' — as 'śukram' pure, 'amṛtam' immortal, that is, as the Brahman expounded above.

The twofold repetition is for the sake of marking the conclusion of the upaniṣad; and the word 'iti' likewise.
Ka_C02_S03_V18: Then Naciketas, having obtained from Death this knowledge and the entire discipline of yoga, attained Brahman and became free from passion and free from death. So too does anyone else become, who knows the Self in this very way.
Ka_C02_S03_V18::block-0:
This concluding statement of the narrative, intended as praise of knowledge, is now spoken — Naciketas, having obtained from Death, by virtue of the boon-granting, this Brahman-knowledge as already expounded, together with the entire discipline of yoga in its completeness, that is, with all its accessories and with its fruit; the word 'lābdhvā' here means 'having obtained' or 'having attained'.

What then? He attained Brahman, that is, he became liberated. How? Through the attainment of knowledge he became 'virajaḥ' — devoid of rajas, devoid of merit and demerit; and 'vimṛtyuḥ' — free from death, free from desire and avidyā, having become so prior to that, is the meaning.

Not only Naciketas alone, but anyone else also who, like Naciketas, is a knower of the Self and knows the inmost Self — that which is the unfigurative, indwelling reality, the very truth that is to be attained — and not any other form which is not the inmost form: he too, knowing the Self in this very way as has been described — such a knower, being devoid of rajas, attains Brahman and becomes free from death. This is the supplementary import of the sentence.
Ka_C02_S03_V19: May He protect us both together. May He nourish us both together. May we both work together with vigour. May our study be radiant. May we never hate each other. Om, peace, peace, peace.
Ka_C02_S03_V19::block-0:
Now this peace-invocation is spoken for the appeasement of any fault arising from inadvertent improper imparting and receiving of knowledge between teacher and disciple — May He protect us both together — that is, may He guard the two of us by manifesting the very nature of knowledge. Who? That very supreme Lord who is revealed by the Upaniṣad.

Further, may He nourish us both together — may He protect the two of us by revealing the fruit thereof. Together let us both bring about the vigour, that is, the capability, born of knowledge — let us accomplish it together. Further, 'tejasvinau' — for the two of us who are radiant, may that which has been studied be well-studied. Or alternatively: 'tejasvi nau' — what has been studied by us two, let it be exceedingly radiant and full of vigour, is the meaning.

'Mā vidviṣāvahai' — let us, teacher and disciple, not bear hatred toward each other on account of any fault arising from inadvertent improper teaching and learning. The thrice-uttered 'śāntiḥ śāntiḥ śāntiḥ' is for the appeasement of all faults.
Ka_C02_S03_V19::block-1: Thus is completed the commentary on the Kāṭhakopaniṣad, composed by the revered Śaṅkara Bhagavat, the disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavatpāda, who is the most exalted teacher among ascetic monks (paramahaṃsa-parivrājakācārya).
